Phonics

Experiment 8 is a phonics lesson on the table-sized phone. The app shows a word split into letter boxes with the sound each spells (c a t, /k/ /æ/ /t/), a hint, a Listen button, a spectrogram panel, a row for what it heard, and a mic button. The fly reads the word and listens while the app plays it (the Listen button animates). The fly stands on the mic button facing up the screen, so the word stays in view while it answers. It presses the mic with a foreleg, holds it down like push-to-talk, and says the word back, its eyes moving across the letter boxes as it goes.

A fly cannot speak, so it sings. Male Drosophila make their courtship song by extending one wing and vibrating it: a pulse song with pulses about 35 ms apart and a sine song humming near 150 Hz. The simulation borrows that. Each sound is buzzed with Web Audio and drawn on the spectrogram from the same model:



Stops (/b d g k p t/): pulse song, three pulses 35 ms apart, band-passed at the consonant's burst frequency.

Vowels (/æ ɛ ɪ ɒ ʌ/): a sawtooth hum at 165 to 205 Hz through two band-pass filters at the vowel's first two formants.

Fricatives (/f s ʃ tʃ h/): noise band-passed around the sound's frequency and fluttered at the wingbeat.

Nasals and liquids (/m n l r/): a low muffled hum, or a gliding one.


In the scene, one wing swings out and vibrates with the sound, and ripples coloured by sound kind spread across the glass. Each sound is right with probability 0.3 + 0.65 × its letter-sound memory. A wrong sound is a plausible confusion (/t/ for /k/, /s/ for /ʃ/, /ɛ/ for /æ/). Each memory learns with Δw = η(R − V). A word gets two attempts; a perfect one earns a dopamine pulse and a celebratory buzz. You hear the buzz while the fly sings, and only then: it is muted between sounds and attempts, when paused, when you switch experiments or views, and when the tab is hidden. The voice is one live synth: a sawtooth wingbeat near 200 Hz, a second wing detuned by under 1 % so the two beat, a wingstroke tremolo, formant filters for vowels, a noise band for fricatives and gated bursts for pulse song. Sound turns on when you open Phonics, since that click lets the browser play audio; the pill above the arena turns it off.

Classroom

Experiment 7 fills a fly-sized classroom: six round tables, four seats each, a tablet in front of every seat, and a whiteboard that tracks the lesson. Twenty-four students, twelve female and twelve male, are seated at random, so some tables are balanced and some are not. The females are drawn larger with a striped, pointed abdomen; the males are smaller, with a dark abdomen tip and sex combs on the forelegs. Every fly has to finish the same twelve word-part items. A lesson ends only when the last fly finishes, then the bell rings and the next lesson starts.

It is mating season, and the flies behave like flies. Each student is a lightweight copy of the procedural fly with its own gait, wings and tapping foreleg, and its own state machine:



On task. It reads its tablet with head sweeps and taps an answer. The chance of a right answer rises with its mastery, learned with the same Δw = η(R − V) rule, and falls when its attention drops.

Courtship. Between items a male may turn toward a female, walk after her (or fly, if she sits at another table), tap her with a foreleg and sing by extending and vibrating one wing.

Rejection. A busy, unreceptive female usually ignores him and keeps tapping, or flicks her wings and kicks, or decamps on a short flight around the room. A female who has finished is more tolerant and may let him stay beside her for a moment. Nothing further happens; he goes back to his tablet.

Courtship conditioning. Each rejection cuts a male's courtship drive by about a third, so the room settles as a lesson goes on. Drive recovers a little between lessons.

Rivals. Two males courting the same female square off with raised wings and lunges, and the loser goes back to his seat.

Grooming and glancing. Flies groom between trials. A fly may glance at a tablemate who is further ahead, which raises the chance that its next answer is right.

Co-action. Attention rises when tablemates are on task and falls when courtship happens at the table or when a male is singing beside you.


Rings under the flies show what each one is doing: blue on task, red courting, pink being courted, amber grooming or glancing, green finished, grey away from the tablet. Dashed red lines join courting pairs, and small badges mark a song, a rejection, a fight or a finished lesson. Toggle that overlay and mating season from the pills above the arena.

With twenty-four flies there is no single fly-eye inset here. Instead, a third pill turns on a computer-vision overlay like the district admin's screen: a bounding box with name and confidence on every fly, its forelegs boxed as hands (filled while tapping), a dashed gaze ray from its head with an eye-contact badge (green on its own tablet, amber on a neighbour's, red when lost to a suitor or rival, grey once done), the last twelve seconds of its path, and a detection summary in the corner.

The camera starts on the whole room; click any fly to follow it and drive the brain panel with its behaviour, which lights the antennal lobes and lateral horn during courtship and the mesothoracic neuropil during song.

Where this sits in the EDLS

The TRD describes a biologically grounded stack: a MuJoCo flybody model (102 DoF, 59 torque channels) driven by a connectome-derived controller (FlyGM on MaleCNS v1.0), with xAPI telemetry flowing through a Science DMZ to a Learning Record Store for G-DINA, Half-Life Regression and Rasch evaluation. This repository implements the interaction layer and a behavioural stand-in for the rest, so the game, camera work, fly-eye optics and brain visualisation can be designed and tested before the heavy components exist.

titles.title: Fruit Fly Lingo

descriptions.description:
Fruit Fly Lingo

A browser simulation of a fruit fly learning to build words. A procedural three.js fly reads a prefix + root + suffix task off a smartphone screen and answers by touching word-part tiles or typing letters, in four student experiments: walking across the phone, flying up to read and diving down to land on its answer, holding a fly-sized phone to swipe and tap, and spelling the word key by key on a laptop. Two more experiments put flies on the other side of the desk: a teacher grading those students from a fly-sized laptop, and a district admin proctoring nine webcam sessions with a vision overlay and an assistant called FlyAI. A side panel shows its central nervous system as a point cloud whose regions light up with what the fly is doing, and a dopamine reward signal that strengthens its memory of each word part.

It is the interactive front end of the Embodied Drosophila Literacy Simulation (EDLS) described in the project's technical requirement document. Everything here is procedural and runs client side in one HTML file; the connectome controller, MuJoCo body and telemetry pipeline from the TRD are the planned back end (see Where this sits in the EDLS).



Running it

Serve the folder over HTTP and open index.html. ES modules and three.js load from jsdelivr, so it needs a server and network access, but no build step.

python3 -m http.server 8000
# then open http://localhost:8000/index.html


Deploying on Vercel

The repository is a static site, so it deploys as is: import it at vercel.com/new, leave the framework preset on "Other" with no build command and the output directory at the repository root, and deploy. vercel.json sets caching for the research PDFs and screenshots. Or use the button:



From a terminal with the Vercel CLI, npx vercel from the repository root does the same.

Trailer



A one-minute trailer (docs/trailer/fruit-fly-lingo-trailer.mp4, 1280 × 720, with sound; a WebM copy is the fallback for browsers without H.264) plays on the home page and near the top of About.




Cold open: a typewriter line, "In a world where fruit flies learn to read…".



Experiments: a 2.4-second shot of each of Experiments 1 to 19, every one a planned camera move timed to the moment the insect is at work. It opens on the fly walking onto the tile that says walk, then:



the page turn with the caterpillar riding it;

the globe spun to Algeria;

algebra typed with the butterfly's abdomen;

the caterpillar holding A for the wave beam.


Each shot has a lower-third caption with a dry joke and a lab-camera HUD (● REC, timecode, specimen, an invented metric).



Dashboards: the live metrics and brain, then two scrolls through the dashboards (one on Δw = η(R − V)).



End card: the title and the address.



The footage was captured from the app itself. Running in a headless browser on a virtual clock, it advanced one frame at a time at 30 fps, so motion is smooth even on a software renderer. The soundtrack is a synthesised chiptune at 100 BPM, so each experiment is one bar and every cut lands on the beat.

Butterfly cut



Teaching a Butterfly How to Read (MP4, WebM) is a one-minute, all-ages cut with no fruit fly in the lead. It plays in the Butterfly mode section of About.



Butterflies: ten experiments, each with a different species, named on its caption.

Caterpillars: after "Then the caterpillars wanted to learn too", six scenes where the caterpillar plays its part: the page turn, math together, retro typing, the arcade, the home console and the maze race.

Ending: the learning dashboards and the maze leaderboard.


Science poster cut



A second one-minute cut for the science poster, Can a fruit fly learn how to read? (MP4, WebM), shows only the fruit fly. It covers the 15 experiments with no butterfly or caterpillar: 1–12, 14, 15 and 17. Each 3.2-second shot sits beside the simulation's own live readouts for that moment:



the rendered fly brain;

a bar chart of activity in each neuropil;

three firing traces (optic lobes, mushroom bodies, leg neuromeres) over the last 3 s;

the PAM dopamine level that drives learning.


It plays at the top of The student experiments on About. It opens with the question and a method card (one simulated brain from the FlyWire and MaleCNS connectomes, fifteen reading tasks, learning by Δw = η(R − V)). It closes on two dashboard scrolls (connectome and psychometrics) and the question again, over a slower 75 BPM score.

Four views

The app is one page with four views, switched by the tabs in the header and by hash routes (#home, #simulate, #dashboards, #about). The home page explains the project and shows a card for each experiment; picking a card opens that experiment in the simulator.

 It works at phone width. The Hide metrics / Show metrics button in the arena hides every panel (the dashboard dock, the bottom strip and the scenario panel) so the 3D view fills the screen; phones start with the metrics hidden, and the choice is remembered. With metrics shown on a phone, the strip and the scenario panel sit under the arena, which keeps at least half the screen. The experiment list scrolls on its own line so speed, camera and Play stay in reach, the camera pulls back on a portrait screen, the fly-eye inset gives way on short screens, and a landscape phone shows only the arena. Controls

The Experiment dropdown in the header lists all twenty experiments in a vertical, scrollable menu (arrow keys, Home, End and Escape work). Camera views: Follow (third person), the experiment's device or scene view, and On its back, which rides just above the fly's or butterfly's thorax, looking forward over its head and eyes at what it is doing; in the classroom it rides on the followed fly. The Hide fly-eye view pill hides the compound-eye inset and is remembered. In butterfly mode a species picker beside the logos dresses every butterfly in every scene: Blue Morpho with the six Gainesville species mixed in the classroom (the default), or any one of Blue Morpho, Zebra Longwing, Gulf Fritillary, Monarch, Eastern Tiger Swallowtail, Cloudless Sulphur and Common Buckeye everywhere.

Rendering: the camera sees 6,000 units with fog from 700, the zoom-out limit is 1,400, and the near clipping plane follows the viewing distance so depth precision is not wasted; every screen, page, card and label drawn on a surface is pulled forward with a polygon offset, which removes the flicker where screens met their bodies. The fly's steps lift fast and set down softly, it rolls a little with the tripod gait, banks into turns in flight, draws its legs in on take-off, its antennae twitch and its abdomen breathes, and its beating wings blur. Its wings are shaped and sized like a Drosophila wing: as long as the body, hinged on the thorax, folded over the abdomen at rest and reaching just past its tip, clear with the costa, veins L2 to L5 and the two crossveins, and a faint iridescence; the body is slimmer to match.

Butterfly mode

The two logos at the left of the header switch the insect. The fruit fly is the default. In butterfly mode every fly in every experiment gets butterfly wings and a bigger body: the student and the VR teacher become Blue Morphos at 1.8 times the fly's size, iridescent blue on top with a black margin and white spots, brown with eyespots underneath. The 24 classroom flies, at 1.3 times, become six species common around Gainesville, Florida, four of each and mixed across the tables: Zebra Longwing (Heliconius charithonia, Florida's state butterfly), Gulf Fritillary (Dione vanillae), Monarch (Danaus plexippus), Eastern Tiger Swallowtail (Papilio glaucus), Cloudless Sulphur (Phoebis sennae) and Common Buckeye (Junonia coenia), each with its own wing shape and upper and under side patterns; the classroom card names the followed butterfly's species. The legs, brain and behaviour stay the same, but the wings change how it moves. At rest it holds them closed over its back, showing the brown undersides, and now and then opens them to bask. It flies with slow, deep strokes, about four a second instead of a fly's two hundred, bobbing up with each downstroke and weaving from side to side. In Phonics it sings by holding one blue wing open, and in the classroom its rejection flicks and threat displays open and close the big wings. The choice is remembered in the browser.

The dashboards

Everything is computed from the live session. Where a quantity stands in for a sensor or model the app does not yet have, the card says so.



Kinematic and sensorimotor. Tarsal adhesion (pads in contact, about 12 µN each), ommatidial contrast sampled from the real screen texture where the head camera's axis meets the glass, a joint-torque proxy from foot speeds, the microsaccadic gaze path drawn on a miniature screen, and viewing distance against the 1 to 10 mm acuity band with an acuity heatmap of where the fly looked while inside it.

Connectomic and neurophysiological. Live afferent, intrinsic and efferent activity as a directed graph coloured by neurotransmitter class; the PAM rule Δw = η(R − V) per answer, which is now the rule the fly's memory actually uses; short-term versus long-term memory traces; a region-to-region connectivity matrix with a MaleCNS v1.0 / FlyWire FAFB toggle (the FAFB view greys out the nerve-cord rows the dataset lacks); a table of which region groups each experiment drives, from the session's mean activity; and a motivation trace of dopamine against every right and wrong answer.

Psychometric and cognitive diagnosis. The Q-matrix from the specification, G-DINA attribute posteriors from session proxies, Half-Life Regression forgetting curves per word part with a configurable P(fail) alert, memory curves for every word part over the session, and a Wright map with the fly's ability θ and its standard error against task difficulties, plus an S-X² misfit flag at 1.5.

Curriculum adaptation. A toy mLSTM cell running the specification's stabilised update on keys from the fly's sensory stream (C_t heat grid, m_t and n_t traces), and the Decision Transformer panel: return-to-go target, difficulty level, and path divergence between the fly's actual path and a ghosted optimal path to the correct tile, which resets the curriculum a level when it exceeds 10. Difficulty changes the distractors: from level 3 they share the needed part's kind.

Spelling

Experiment 4 is a fourth literacy activity. The real-size laptop shows the meaning to spell and the three word-part hints with their glosses, then a row of letter boxes underlined by part. The fly hovers in front of the screen to read, then flies to the key for the next letter and presses it with its whole body. The chance of the right key grows with the memory of the word part the letter belongs to; a wrong choice lands on a neighbouring key, flashes red, and counts as a wrong answer. Each letter is a trial like a tile press, so it feeds the same memory rule, dashboards, and the teacher's roster, where the speller is Fly D.

Teacher

Experiment 5 turns the study on itself. A teacher fly sits at a fly-sized laptop (smaller than the phone in Experiment 3) running a small learning-management gradebook whose students are Fly A, B, C and D: the walking, flying, touch and spelling flies from Experiments 1 to 4. Their rows are this session's real trials (answers, accuracy, words built, word-part memory), so what the teacher reads is the ongoing study. For each student the teacher reads the gradebook, opens the row, reads the detail page, clicks the grade field, types a grade equal to what it believes the student's accuracy is (it misreads digits less as it practises), presses Enter and clicks Submit; a student with no submission yet is marked Incomplete. When all four are graded a new grading period opens.

The screen is never touched and there is no mouse. The teacher parks at the back of the trackpad and steers the cursor with one foreleg inside a reach window that maps onto the whole screen, so the entire trackpad is covered by moving one leg; a press of the pad is a click, and the movement time of each steer follows the target's index of difficulty. It leaves the pad only to step over to a key, tap it, and walk back.

District admin

Experiment 6 puts an admin fly at the same fly-sized laptop, trackpad only, in front of a proctoring screen: a 3 × 3 grid of webcam sessions, three each of walking, flying and touch students, each a lightweight simulation with its own phone, answers and behaviour. Three of the nine are seeded each session with a cheating behaviour: looking away from the task, a helper fly in frame, a second device, or answering while off camera. Honest students still glance away now and then.

A computer-vision overlay runs on every tile: a bounding box on the fly with a confidence score, boxes on both forelegs labelled hands, and a dashed gaze ray with an eye-contact badge that turns red when the gaze leaves the student's own screen, plus badges for a second fly, a second device or an off-camera fly. FlyAI, a rule-based assistant in a chat panel, reads that evidence and posts flags with the student's attention and accuracy and a recommendation. The admin watches the grid, steers the cursor to a flagged tile, opens it, and clicks the check-in button; a check-in stops the behaviour for a while.

Dashboard 6, District proctoring, scores the flags against the hidden seeding: confirmed flags and false alarms, precision, cheaters caught, response time from flag to check-in, attention per student (with the seeded names marked in red, which the admin never sees), detection counts over time, and the FlyAI log.

Geography

Experiment 15 is trivia on a globe. The globe stands on a school desk, tilted 23.4° in a brass meridian ring and drawn with real country outlines: Natural Earth at 1:110m, vendored from the world-atlas package as docs/geo/countries-110m.json (ISC licence, docs/geo/LICENSE-world-atlas) and decoded from TopoJSON in the page. A trivia card on the desk asks one of 49 questions, such as "Machu Picchu sits high in the mountains of which country?".

The fly walks to the card and reads it, flies to the globe and sweeps it round with a foreleg until the region it wants faces it, then flies to the country and taps it. The country lights green if it is right; if it is wrong it lights red, the right country lights green, and the distance between them is measured along the Earth's surface. The chance of choosing the right country is 0.3 + 0.65 × its memory, learned with Δw = η(R − V); a wrong choice is one of the four countries nearest the right one. Questions come in rounds of ten. The Globe camera button frames the globe, and Dashboard 15 keeps countries right, distance off, country memory and every answer.

Arcade

Experiment 18 stands an upright 80s arcade cabinet on the floor: a classic silhouette (kick panel, control panel lip, screen sloping back, marquee overhang), a lit marquee, a coin door with glowing slots and INSERT COIN, a control panel with a ball-top joystick and A and B buttons, and a portrait CRT tilted back in its bezel. It runs Root Blaster, a 2D pixel shooter at 224 × 288 with hard pixels, in the style of the formation-and-dive and centipede-in-the-mushrooms classics, with original sprites and no maker's names. A starfield scrolls behind a swaying formation of bug sprites, each carrying a word part; now and then one peels off and dives at the ship. Below them a centipede winds down through a field of coloured mushrooms, turning a row lower at every wall and mushroom, splitting when hit and leaving a mushroom where a segment dies. The meaning to build and three slots sit under the score.

The game borrows from the side-scrolling shooters too, so there is always something happening:



Scenery. A slowly shifting nebula painted in chunky pixels, three layers of stars, a ringed planet drifting past, and organic walls with glowing eye pods scrolling down both edges.

Force pod. An orange pod rides in front of the ship. Shots leave from it as blue ripples, and it soaks up the bugs' return fire.

Wave beam. Holding A charges the BEAM meter at the bottom. On release a twisting beam cuts through everything in its column. Every fourth shot the insect lines up is a charged one, so the caterpillar holds the button down for a second.

Boss. After every second word a WARNING card brings in the Root Hydra: a ribbed carapace with an eye that opens and closes, waving tentacles and a fan of shots. It takes 30 hits (a beam does 6) and goes down in a chain of explosions, then the STAGE 2 card names the next stage.

Effects. Bugs flap their wings, diving bugs leave trails, explosions throw sparks and a shock ring and shake the screen, and points float up where they were scored. Capsules flash, WORD BUILT is in rainbow letters with fireworks, and faint scanlines sit over everything.


Both cabinet sides carry the game's promotional art, painted to the side's shape: a synthwave sky with a striped sun and neon mountains over a pink perspective grid, a giant centipede coiling down the upper column through pixel bugs while the ship blasts it with twin lasers, and a chrome ROOT BLASTER logo with the tagline BLAST THE ROOTS · BUILD THE WORDS. The left side mirrors the scene to fit its silhouette but keeps the lettering readable.

The arcade has its own sound effects, synthesised live in the browser with Web Audio and no sound files: a laser zap for every shot, a crack when a bug is hit and an explosion as it bursts, a pop for each centipede segment, a tick on mushrooms, a falling whistle when a bug dives, a chime for the right part, a buzz for the wrong one, a jingle for WORD BUILT, a long crash when the ship is lost, a blip for each enemy shot, a rising whine while the beam charges, a roar when it fires, a siren for the WARNING and a rolling explosion when the boss goes down. Sound turns on when Experiment 18 opens (the browser may wait for a first click); the Sound button turns it off.

The insect stands on the control panel, reared up with both forelegs on the joystick ball; the stick tilts as it pushes and the insect leans with it. It steers the ship under the bug carrying the part it chose (the choice comes from the word-part memory shared with Experiments 1 to 4), and the caterpillar, sitting by the A button, bonks it with its head to fire, two shots at most on screen. Choosing a leaf. It goes for the nearest right leaf with a chance of 0.45 + 0.5 × its memory of that part, and otherwise for a nearby decoy.

Getting there. A shortest-path search takes it round the hedges, steering clear of corridors other bodies lie in when there is another way. Its body follows the head's own trail, so it bends round corners.

Traffic. It pauses at a head-on jam. When two meet, the one arriving arches its body over the other.

Eating. It rears up to munch for a moment. The leaf shrinks with each bite, and a green +1 or a red ✗ floats up.

Learning. Each caterpillar has its own word-part memory, updated with Δw = η(R − V), so the eight learn at their own pace.

Experiment 13 is a match: the fruit fly against a Blue Morpho butterfly on a full 15 by 15 board, with the standard premium squares, letter values and a 98-tile bag (no blanks). Each player starts knowing the two- and three-letter words and about half of the rest of a 500-word list, and finds every legal placement of the words it knows. It plays its best-scoring word six times in ten and one of its top five otherwise, swaps three tiles when it finds nothing, and learns seven in ten of the words its opponent plays. Writing

Experiment 10 is a cursive writing app on the table-sized phone. It asks about twelve Greek roots, alternating between "What does the Greek root bio mean?" and "Which Greek root means light?", with example words such as biology and photograph, and gives lined handwriting paper, a readout of what the recogniser read, and Clear and Submit buttons.

The fly answers in joined cursive with the tip of its abdomen, while flying. It hovers over the question to read it, then flies down and pitches about 29° nose-up so that its abdomen tip rests on the glass, and follows each letter's stroke at about 90 px a second, laying ink behind it. It lifts the tip to hop to the dot of an i or the cross of a t. The letter shapes are the Hershey Script 1-stroke font, a public-domain single-stroke font made for pen plotters (via the MIT-licensed hersheytext package); only the 26 lowercase glyphs are embedded, about 3 KB. The abdominal ganglion lights up in the brain panel while it writes.

Hovering flight adds a smooth wobble to the line, which shrinks as the fly's tail control improves with each answer. When it taps Submit the recogniser reads the handwriting; very shaky writing, below about 55 % legibility, can turn one letter into another. Whether the answer itself is right depends on a memory per root, learned with Δw = η(R − V); a wrong answer is another root's meaning, another root, or a dropped letter.

Phonics

Experiment 8 is a phonics lesson on the table-sized phone. The app shows a word split into letter boxes with the sound each spells (c a t, /k/ /æ/ /t/), a hint, a Listen button, a spectrogram panel, a row for what it heard, and a mic button. The fly reads the word and listens while the app plays it (the Listen button animates). The fly stands on the mic button facing up the screen, so the word stays in view while it answers. It presses the mic with a foreleg, holds it down like push-to-talk, and says the word back, its eyes moving across the letter boxes as it goes.

A fly cannot speak, so it sings. Male Drosophila make their courtship song by extending one wing and vibrating it: a pulse song with pulses about 35 ms apart and a sine song humming near 150 Hz. The simulation borrows that. Each sound is buzzed with Web Audio and drawn on the spectrogram from the same model:



Stops (/b d g k p t/): pulse song, three pulses 35 ms apart, band-passed at the consonant's burst frequency.

Vowels (/æ ɛ ɪ ɒ ʌ/): a sawtooth hum at 165 to 205 Hz through two band-pass filters at the vowel's first two formants.

Fricatives (/f s ʃ tʃ h/): noise band-passed around the sound's frequency and fluttered at the wingbeat.

Nasals and liquids (/m n l r/): a low muffled hum, or a gliding one.


In the scene, one wing swings out and vibrates with the sound, and ripples coloured by sound kind spread across the glass. Each sound is right with probability 0.3 + 0.65 × its letter-sound memory. A wrong sound is a plausible confusion (/t/ for /k/, /s/ for /ʃ/, /ɛ/ for /æ/). Each memory learns with Δw = η(R − V). A word gets two attempts; a perfect one earns a dopamine pulse and a celebratory buzz. You hear the buzz while the fly sings, and only then: it is muted between sounds and attempts, when paused, when you switch experiments or views, and when the tab is hidden. The voice is one live synth: a sawtooth wingbeat near 200 Hz, a second wing detuned by under 1 % so the two beat, a wingstroke tremolo, formant filters for vowels, a noise band for fricatives and gated bursts for pulse song. Sound turns on when you open Phonics, since that click lets the browser play audio; the pill above the arena turns it off.

Classroom

Experiment 7 fills a fly-sized classroom: six round tables, four seats each, a tablet in front of every seat, and a whiteboard that tracks the lesson. Twenty-four students, twelve female and twelve male, are seated at random, so some tables are balanced and some are not. The females are drawn larger with a striped, pointed abdomen; the males are smaller, with a dark abdomen tip and sex combs on the forelegs. Every fly has to finish the same twelve word-part items. A lesson ends only when the last fly finishes, then the bell rings and the next lesson starts.

It is mating season, and the flies behave like flies. Each student is a lightweight copy of the procedural fly with its own gait, wings and tapping foreleg, and its own state machine:



On task. It reads its tablet with head sweeps and taps an answer. The chance of a right answer rises with its mastery, learned with the same Δw = η(R − V) rule, and falls when its attention drops.

Courtship. Between items a male may turn toward a female, walk after her (or fly, if she sits at another table), tap her with a foreleg and sing by extending and vibrating one wing.

Rejection. A busy, unreceptive female usually ignores him and keeps tapping, or flicks her wings and kicks, or decamps on a short flight around the room. A female who has finished is more tolerant and may let him stay beside her for a moment. Nothing further happens; he goes back to his tablet.

Courtship conditioning. Each rejection cuts a male's courtship drive by about a third, so the room settles as a lesson goes on. Drive recovers a little between lessons.

Rivals. Two males courting the same female square off with raised wings and lunges, and the loser goes back to his seat.

Grooming and glancing. Flies groom between trials. A fly may glance at a tablemate who is further ahead, which raises the chance that its next answer is right.

Co-action. Attention rises when tablemates are on task and falls when courtship happens at the table or when a male is singing beside you.


Rings under the flies show what each one is doing: blue on task, red courting, pink being courted, amber grooming or glancing, green finished, grey away from the tablet. Dashed red lines join courting pairs, and small badges mark a song, a rejection, a fight or a finished lesson. Toggle that overlay and mating season from the pills above the arena.

With twenty-four flies there is no single fly-eye inset here. Instead, a third pill turns on a computer-vision overlay like the district admin's screen: a bounding box with name and confidence on every fly, its forelegs boxed as hands (filled while tapping), a dashed gaze ray from its head with an eye-contact badge (green on its own tablet, amber on a neighbour's, red when lost to a suitor or rival, grey once done), the last twelve seconds of its path, and a detection summary in the corner.

The camera starts on the whole room; click any fly to follow it and drive the brain panel with its behaviour, which lights the antennal lobes and lateral horn during courtship and the mesothoracic neuropil during song.

The TRD describes a biologically grounded stack: a MuJoCo flybody model (102 DoF, 59 torque channels) driven by a connectome-derived controller (FlyGM on MaleCNS v1.0), with xAPI telemetry flowing through a Science DMZ to a Learning Record Store for G-DINA, Half-Life Regression and Rasch evaluation. Design system

Styling uses a University of Florida palette: core blue for actions, dark blue for chrome and text, alachua for work in flight, gator green for mastery, and bottlebrush red only for errors. titles.title: GROWING OYSTER MUSHROOMS: A STARTER GUIDE FOR FIRST-TIME GROWERS

dates.dateInformation: A practical guide ebook for first time oyster mushrooms growers

rightsList.rights: Creative Commons Attribution Non Commercial No Derivatives 4.0 International

descriptions.description:
A short, free introductory guide to growing oyster mushrooms (Pleurotus spp.) for first-time and small-scale growers.The guide teaches the shape of the craft rather than a recipe: what the oyster mushroom is and why it is a forgiving first crop; the two phases of cultivation — colonisation and fruiting — that organise everything a grower does; the six needs (food, moisture, mild temperatures, fresh air, light and hygiene); the cultivation cycle from substrate preparation to harvest; the mistakes almost every beginner makes; post-harvest handling and drying; and the record-keeping habit that separates growers from amateurs.It is deliberately light on figures. A number without its context is a trap in cultivation — the right temperature for one variety is the wrong one for another — so the guide explains why figures matter before it offers any, and the few indicative anchors it does give are labelled as orientation rather than protocol. It is written to be read in an evening.No primary experimental data are reported. The photographs are the author's own cultivation records, together with a small number of AI-generated illustrations for steps the author had not photographed; each AI-generated image is labelled in its caption. The guidance is general information, not professional advice.This guide is the practical companion to the author's narrative review of the published literature on the subject: Rathore, S. (2026). Cultivation of Oyster Mushroom (Pleurotus spp.) in Hot Semi-Arid Regions: A Narrative Review. Preprint. (https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7587518).Free to read and share; not for resale. First edition, October 2026.

A commercial Kindle edition is available on Amazon: https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0H3CG78K4

titles.title: Neural Metamorphosis: Highway Hijacking, State- Congruent Loading, and the Civic Architecture of Accelerated Human Learning

descriptions.description:
Abstract

The first part of Under the Broken Halo set out the SEIR cognitive loop (Sensory experience, Experience encoding, Interpretation, Response) as a universal architecture of antisocial behaviour, defined Loop Lock as the state in which a recursive system can no longer update its model of the world, and ended with a three-phase surgical hypothesis built on molecular engram ablation and symmetry-location neural cartography. The second part tested that architecture against forty-four documented lives across twenty-three centuries and found the predicted sequence intact, together with a finding that constrains everything written here: every documented opening of a locked loop followed a sustained change of environment over time, and none followed punishment or argument alone.

This third part turns from removal to replacement. Where Part One targeted pathological pathways for elimination, the framework set out here leaves the pathway standing and changes what runs on it. The governing mechanism is Highway Hijacking: the hyper-myelinated, metabolically privileged circuits built by trauma, compulsion, hypervigilance, craving, or any other high-intensity experience are not destroyed, and the historical memory attached to them is not touched. What is replaced is the recurring traffic — the rumination, the rehearsed grievance, the intrusive loop — and what replaces it is structured knowledge delivered under four rules: State-Congruent Loading, which matches the content of the upload to the emotional state that built the pathway; Paired Loading, which activates a regulating region alongside the primary skill so that the brake is wired at the same moment as the engine; the Chrysalis sequence, which consolidates each session in protected rest; and daily repetition at a fixed hour until the new traffic is established. The axiom beneath all four is drawn from Part One: people are the product of what they perceive, and what you learn, you become.

The second half of this paper is institutional rather than technical, because the history assembled in Under the Devil's Halo establishes that a benevolent technology without a civic architecture becomes a coercive one within a generation. Three delivery structures are set out: a voluntary school of cognitive learning entered at university age; a correctional pathway restricted to lower-tier violent offences and offered, never imposed, with the most serious categories of crime left entirely inside ordinary criminal law; and a clinical pathway for people whose trauma, addiction, or compulsion produces severe documented suffering. Each inherits the guardrails of Part One, Chapter 9, and each is measured against the eight principles for honest help set out in Under the Devil's Halo. The paper states its open questions rather than concealing them, and it accepts the constraint that its own case evidence imposes: this is accelerated, structured consolidation, not instantaneous transfer.

 

I. The Moth in the Cocoon

In 2008, Douglas Blackiston, Elena Silva Casey, and Martha Weiss trained tobacco hornworm caterpillars to avoid a specific odour by pairing that odour with a mild electric shock. The caterpillars learned. Then they did what caterpillars do: they entered the pupal stage, during which large portions of the nervous system are broken down and rebuilt into something structurally and behaviourally unrecognisable. When the adult moths emerged, they still avoided the odour. The aversion had survived a reconstruction of the animal that produced it.

Two details of that experiment matter more than the headline. The first is timing: caterpillars trained in early larval stages did not retain the aversion, while those trained in the final stages did, and the researchers connected this to regions of the mushroom bodies — the insect's learning centres — that persist through metamorphosis rather than being dismantled. What survives a transformation is not everything learned, but what was consolidated deeply enough before the transformation began. The second detail is the nature of the learning itself. The caterpillars did not learn in a state of calm. They learned under aversive conditioning, with the odour bound to a noxious stimulus. What travelled across the cocoon was a fear association.

Both details carry directly into human terms, and they cut in two directions at once. The encouraging reading is that learning can survive the most radical structural reorganisation an animal nervous system undergoes, which means that deliberately written content has a biological precedent for persistence. The sobering reading is the mirror image: if an aversion written under stress survives a nervous system being rebuilt, then a human trauma written under adrenaline and cortisol will not be dissolved by any process that merely reorganises structure. Stress hormones, acting through the amygdala, strengthen consolidation rather than weakening it, which is why emotionally charged memories are among the most durable a person carries. Any framework that treats a traumatic circuit as fragile has misread the biology at the outset.

The architecture set out in this paper takes both readings seriously. It does not attempt to dissolve what trauma wrote. It works on the assumption that the pathway is permanent, that the memory attached to it is permanent, and that the only thing genuinely available for change is what runs along the pathway from one day to the next. The cocoon supplies the other half of the design. The caterpillar does not rebuild itself while fleeing a predator. It rebuilds in a sealed, protected, resting state, with the outside world held at a distance. The trauma was written in alarm; the rewriting is sealed in rest. That asymmetry is not decorative. It is the operating principle of the entire protocol, and it appears in this paper as the Chrysalis phase.

The second part of Under the Broken Halo documented the human version of the moth's journey without naming it as such. Carl Panzram's reform school was written into a child and acted out by a man in a different country decades later. Jean-Bédel Bokassa's father was beaten to death at a colonial administrative post when Bokassa was six, and the scene was reproduced, with the roles exchanged, against the children of his own country more than half a century afterwards. Harold Shipman watched a doctor administer morphine to his dying mother at seventeen, and the configuration of that room — the physician, the syringe, the older woman, the home — was reproduced hundreds of times across a medical career. In each case the person who acted was, in every ordinary sense, a different person from the child who encoded the material. The body had changed, the circumstances had changed, the social role had changed entirely. The encoding travelled anyway. Inherited trauma does not remain a memory of an event. It becomes identity, and identity is what survives transformation.

That last point governs the ethics of everything that follows, and it is the reason this framework abandoned the removal strategy of Part One. If what sits on these pathways has become identity, then eliminating it is not a repair. It is a subtraction from the person, and the lobotomy record assembled in Part One, Chapter 9 documents in detail what subtraction from a person looks like when an institution performs it for the person's own good. The alternative pursued here adds rather than subtracts. Nothing is taken out. The highway stays, the memory stays, the person stays, and new traffic is given to a road that was already carrying something destructive.

 

II. Highway Hijacking: The Core Mechanism

1. What Is Actually Being Changed

The language of "uploading" invites a misreading that the rest of this paper works to prevent. Nothing is downloaded into a brain the way a file is written to a disk, and the framework here makes no claim that a memory can be deleted, overwritten, or replaced by an external data payload.

titles.title: PREreview of "Stochastic splicing and deterministic inclusion of variable exons promote diversification of Down Syndrome Cell Adhesion Molecule expression"

descriptions.description:
This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/23397337.


Lassota and colleagues ask whether the selection of Dscam variable exons is really the stochastic process the field has assumed. They build a dual-amplification splicing reporter for the Drosophila exon 9 cluster, in which a single-nucleotide deletion places one variant in frame with LexA, so that inclusion of that variant drives a LexAop reporter through a GAL4 cascade. Applied to third instar tissues, the reporters give patterned rather than random output: segmentally reiterated rows of cells in the ventral nerve cord, enrichment in the mushroom body neuroblast region for exon 4, and repeated labelling of the same positional photoreceptor across ommatidia. Against this, the authors find that reporter expression is markedly heterogeneous between salivary gland cells even when all 33 variants are in frame, and that the terminal intron of the cluster is retained more in salivary glands than in the VNC. In honey bees, FISH against variable exons 4.5, 4.7, 10.10 and 10.15 shows broad uniform signal in newly emerged workers and compartmentalised signal in foragers, with patterns differing between the two mushroom bodies of the same brain, and a 2-phenylethanol exposure paradigm reproduces the shift within 24 to 48 hours.


The advance is conceptual as much as technical. The field has treated "stochastic" as a single property of exon choice. This work separates it into two: whether the cluster is spliced through productively, which varies between genotypically identical cells, and which variant is selected given that it is, which appears biased by lineage, cell type and compartment. The all-in-frame control is the key piece of evidence, since a dark cell there cannot be explained by a different variant having been chosen, and exon 9 variants preserve frame so skipping is also excluded. The bee data then add a layer the fly work cannot reach, showing that the spatial organisation of inclusion is not fixed at differentiation but is rewritten by sensory experience over a day or two. Together these results give a more tractable model than "each neuron rolls the dice," and the reporter itself will be useful to others working on low-abundance isoforms.


Major issues


Absence of reporter signal is read throughout as absence of productive splicing, but the detection threshold of a two-step amplification system is never characterised. This is most consequential for the optic lobe claim. The authors concede the general point themselves when they attribute the larval to pupal photoreceptor difference to amplification delay. The qRT-PCR assay in Figure 2X–Y is the obvious fix: run it on dissected optic lobe against central brain, and the claim stops depending on a negative image.


The HA and FLAG logic does not work as drawn. In Figure 1B, FLAG sits downstream of the 2A peptide and in frame with LexA, so FLAG positivity is itself conditional on productive splicing and cannot serve as an independent check that the transgene is expressed. "All FLAG-positive cells expressed the reporter" is close to circular. The eye disc result then describes the opposite relationship, with FLAG ubiquitous and HA tracking the reporter, which is inconsistent both with the salivary glands and with the construct.


Figure 2W compares variance between two different reporter systems. elav>H2B::YFP involves one transcriptional step; the exon 9 reporter involves two, with a different fluorophore and different protein stability. These will differ in variance for reasons unrelated to splicing. The appropriate comparison is a UAS-LexA construct lacking the variable cluster, read out through the same LexAop line. If that line does not exist, the argument should rest on the qRT-PCR, which is not vulnerable to this.


The NMJ experiment lacks its genetic controls. Only wild type is shown. Driver-alone and RNAi-alone heterozygotes on RU486 are needed, knockdown efficiency should be documented at the two day timepoint, and bouton counts should be normalised to muscle area. There is also a flat contradiction in the text: line 258 reports a significant reduction in bouton number, while the heading, the figure, the legend and the abstract all report an increase. This inverts the conclusion and needs fixing.


Age and experience are confounded in Figures 5 and 6, since naïve bees are dissected within 24 h of emergence and foragers are weeks older. The authors half acknowledge this and the odour experiment does most of the work of separating them, but the wording in those sections should reflect it. Relatedly, "compartmentalised" is scored by eye from representative images. Defining the compartments anatomically, extracting intensity profiles normalised to the constant region probe, and having a blinded scorer classify the images would convert an impression into a measurement without much additional work.


One probe control is missing. The cross-species negative and the complexin comparison are both good, but the real risk with variable exons is cross-hybridisation between paralogous variants of the same cluster, which nothing currently addresses. Showing that two variant probes give non-overlapping patterns in the same brain would settle it.


Minor issues




The bee exon 10 cluster and the fly exon 9 cluster are orthologous; say so at first mention, because readers will otherwise read it as an error.

Methods list a probe against exon 10.2 (line 547) that never appears in the results. Presumably 10.15.

Figure 2W marks p = 0.0059 with two asterisks defined as p ≤ 0.001.

Supplementary Figure 4, the three schematic models, frames the entire paper and would do more work in the main text.

For the salivary gland comparison, give n for both nuclei and glands, and state whether nuclei were nested within glands in the analysis.

titles.title: PREreview of "Stochastic splicing and deterministic inclusion of variable exons promote diversification of Down Syndrome Cell Adhesion Molecule expression"

descriptions.description:
This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/23397337.


Lassota and colleagues ask whether the selection of Dscam variable exons is really the stochastic process the field has assumed. They build a dual-amplification splicing reporter for the Drosophila exon 9 cluster, in which a single-nucleotide deletion places one variant in frame with LexA, so that inclusion of that variant drives a LexAop reporter through a GAL4 cascade. Applied to third instar tissues, the reporters give patterned rather than random output: segmentally reiterated rows of cells in the ventral nerve cord, enrichment in the mushroom body neuroblast region for exon 4, and repeated labelling of the same positional photoreceptor across ommatidia. Against this, the authors find that reporter expression is markedly heterogeneous between salivary gland cells even when all 33 variants are in frame, and that the terminal intron of the cluster is retained more in salivary glands than in the VNC. In honey bees, FISH against variable exons 4.5, 4.7, 10.10 and 10.15 shows broad uniform signal in newly emerged workers and compartmentalised signal in foragers, with patterns differing between the two mushroom bodies of the same brain, and a 2-phenylethanol exposure paradigm reproduces the shift within 24 to 48 hours.


The advance is conceptual as much as technical. The field has treated "stochastic" as a single property of exon choice. This work separates it into two: whether the cluster is spliced through productively, which varies between genotypically identical cells, and which variant is selected given that it is, which appears biased by lineage, cell type and compartment. The all-in-frame control is the key piece of evidence, since a dark cell there cannot be explained by a different variant having been chosen, and exon 9 variants preserve frame so skipping is also excluded. The bee data then add a layer the fly work cannot reach, showing that the spatial organisation of inclusion is not fixed at differentiation but is rewritten by sensory experience over a day or two. Together these results give a more tractable model than "each neuron rolls the dice," and the reporter itself will be useful to others working on low-abundance isoforms.


Major issues


Absence of reporter signal is read throughout as absence of productive splicing, but the detection threshold of a two-step amplification system is never characterised. This is most consequential for the optic lobe claim. The authors concede the general point themselves when they attribute the larval to pupal photoreceptor difference to amplification delay. The qRT-PCR assay in Figure 2X–Y is the obvious fix: run it on dissected optic lobe against central brain, and the claim stops depending on a negative image.


The HA and FLAG logic does not work as drawn. In Figure 1B, FLAG sits downstream of the 2A peptide and in frame with LexA, so FLAG positivity is itself conditional on productive splicing and cannot serve as an independent check that the transgene is expressed. "All FLAG-positive cells expressed the reporter" is close to circular. The eye disc result then describes the opposite relationship, with FLAG ubiquitous and HA tracking the reporter, which is inconsistent both with the salivary glands and with the construct.


Figure 2W compares variance between two different reporter systems. elav>H2B::YFP involves one transcriptional step; the exon 9 reporter involves two, with a different fluorophore and different protein stability. These will differ in variance for reasons unrelated to splicing. The appropriate comparison is a UAS-LexA construct lacking the variable cluster, read out through the same LexAop line. If that line does not exist, the argument should rest on the qRT-PCR, which is not vulnerable to this.


The NMJ experiment lacks its genetic controls. Only wild type is shown. Driver-alone and RNAi-alone heterozygotes on RU486 are needed, knockdown efficiency should be documented at the two day timepoint, and bouton counts should be normalised to muscle area. There is also a flat contradiction in the text: line 258 reports a significant reduction in bouton number, while the heading, the figure, the legend and the abstract all report an increase. This inverts the conclusion and needs fixing.


Age and experience are confounded in Figures 5 and 6, since naïve bees are dissected within 24 h of emergence and foragers are weeks older. The authors half acknowledge this and the odour experiment does most of the work of separating them, but the wording in those sections should reflect it. Relatedly, "compartmentalised" is scored by eye from representative images. Defining the compartments anatomically, extracting intensity profiles normalised to the constant region probe, and having a blinded scorer classify the images would convert an impression into a measurement without much additional work.


One probe control is missing. The cross-species negative and the complexin comparison are both good, but the real risk with variable exons is cross-hybridisation between paralogous variants of the same cluster, which nothing currently addresses. Showing that two variant probes give non-overlapping patterns in the same brain would settle it.


Minor issues




The bee exon 10 cluster and the fly exon 9 cluster are orthologous; say so at first mention, because readers will otherwise read it as an error.

Methods list a probe against exon 10.2 (line 547) that never appears in the results. Presumably 10.15.

Figure 2W marks p = 0.0059 with two asterisks defined as p ≤ 0.001.

Supplementary Figure 4, the three schematic models, frames the entire paper and would do more work in the main text.

For the salivary gland comparison, give n for both nuclei and glands, and state whether nuclei were nested within glands in the analysis.




The claim that reduced Dscam in fly motor neurons is "consistent with enhanced memory" links two species and two paradigms fairly loosely. Flag it as speculation.

descriptions.description: This dataset contains the experimental data supporting the study “Krüppel Regulates Cell Cycle Exit and Limits Adult Neurogenesis of Mushroom Body Neural Progenitors in Drosophila.” The dataset includes quantitative and imaging data generated from Drosophila melanogaster brain samples, including measurements of neuroblast proliferation, MBNB persistence, cell-cycle activity, Kr, Imp, Syp, E93 and Kr-h1 expression, as well as mushroom body morphology and related phenotypes. These data support the investigation of the role of Krüppel and Krüppel homolog 1 in regulating mushroom body neuroblast cell-cycle exit, elimination, temporal progression and adult neurogenic potential. The dataset is provided to facilitate transparency, reproducibility, and further research.

titles.title: 3D Gaussian Splatting from RGB-D Input for Enhanced Scene Modelling

descriptions.description:
MSc dissertation in Artificial Intelligence, University of Surrey (September 2026). Supervised by Dr Jean-Yves Guillemaut.

3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) enables real-time, high-fidelity novel-view synthesis, but its photometric optimisation can leave geometry under-constrained. Existing depth-aware methods often alter initialisation, supervision, and densification together, making their individual contributions difficult to isolate.

This dissertation introduces Matched-Admission Depth-Guided Spawning (MA-DGS), a densification mechanism that uses depth-conditioned, contour-informed candidate selection and places new Gaussians at back-projected sensor depth. At each densification round, MA-DGS requests the same number of spawns as standard density control admits, avoiding an absolute threshold on a differently scaled signal. Its effects are isolated through two controlled 2×2 factorial studies: one crossing initialisation with depth supervision, and the other crossing depth-guided placement with depth supervision. Each condition is evaluated using three seeds on three MuSHRoom scenes. A depth-ranked matched-admission variant, MA-DGD, is included as a control, and the proposed configuration is compared with a reproduction of DN-Splatter using its official implementation.

Relative to the corresponding standard-density-control baselines, MA-DGS improves all three image-quality metrics in every scene and supervision regime, significantly so for SSIM and LPIPS throughout and for PSNR wherever depth supervision is absent. It reduces LPIPS by 25–29% with depth supervision and 35–44% without it, significantly increases SSIM throughout, and improves PSNR by 0.9–2.8 dB without supervision and by up to 0.3 dB with it. Depth supervision provides the largest geometric gain, reducing absolute relative depth error (AbsRel) by up to 90%. MA-DGS additionally reduces AbsRel by 30–53% without depth supervision, but this geometric effect becomes statistically undetectable once supervision is enabled, while its perceptual benefit remains significant. Dense initialisation improves PSNR by 0.4–0.8 dB without depth supervision and by up to 0.3 dB with it, whereas MA-DGD produces no detectable improvement.

The proposed configuration (SfM initialisation, depth supervision, and MA-DGS) outperforms the DN-Splatter reproduction in PSNR by 1.3–1.4 dB and achieves higher SSIM on all three scenes. DN-Splatter achieves better AbsRel and δ1 throughout, and better LPIPS on two scenes. Overall, matched-admission depth-guided placement consistently improves photometric quality across PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS, while its additional geometric benefit is confined to settings without depth supervision.

titles.title: Characteristic Secondary Metabolites Dataset of Poisonous Mushrooms

descriptions.description: This dataset collects standardized toxicological records for characteristic secondary metabolites derived from poisonous mushrooms, as well as related compounds. It comprises three Excel files (in .xlsx format):Compounds.xlsx (678 records): Contains chemical information for each compound, including common name, chemical taxonomy, PubChem CID, ChEBI ID, CAS number, synonyms, molecular formula, SMILES, InChI, InChIKey, and physicochemical properties.Mushrooms.xlsx (235 records): Provides taxonomic details of mushroom species, including fungus name, synonyms or previously used names, taxonomic classification, NCBI Taxonomy ID, and associated compound names.ToxicityData.xlsx (915 records): Each record links a compound to a literature reference. Toxicity data are organized into three levels:General toxicityOrgan toxicity (subdivided into hepatotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, gastrointestinal toxicity, neurotoxicity, and other toxicities)CytotoxicityFor quantitative endpoints (e.g., IC50, EC50, LD50), the dataset standardizes key information including parameter type, value, unit, administration route, experimental model, and source reference. Descriptive information (e.g., organ injury manifestations, toxicity characteristics, mechanisms of action) is recorded as free text and linked to the original reference. This dataset supports research in mushroom poisoning, natural product toxicology, and drug safety.

titles.title: PMMdb: Poisonous Mushroom Metabolites Dataset

descriptions.description: PMMdb is a curated dataset linking poisonous-mushroom metabolites with source taxa and toxicological evidence. This release contains 674 compounds, 235 mushroom taxa, 1,043 literature-supported compound–species associations, and 915 experimental toxicity records. Data are provided as eight relational TSV tables, an SDF structure file, an accompanying Data Dictionary, and a machine-readable validation summary reporting the main technical validation results. These files support transparent data retrieval, evidence tracing, quality assessment, toxicological research, and computational reuse.

subjects.subject: soil health; Haney Soil Health Tool; organic amendments; nutrient availability; soil nutrient cycling; apple orchard; reproducible research

descriptions.description:
This repository contains the dataset and reproducible R workflow associated with a four-year field experiment evaluating complementary outputs of the Haney Soil Health Tool (HSHT) in two commercial apple orchards under organic and conventional management in northern Italy. Three organic amendments (digestate, green compost, and mushroom compost) were evaluated against orchard-specific controls in randomized complete block designs with four independent replicates per treatment. The two orchards represent distinct experimental contexts and were analyzed independently; they should not be treated as replicated levels of orchard management.

The repository includes the plot-level dataset, a data dictionary, R scripts for data validation and processing, statistical analysis, and figure generation, machine-readable statistical outputs, final figures, and information on the R computational environment. The workflow independently recalculates and validates derived HSHT variables before reproducing the statistical analyses and figures associated with the manuscript.

The research data, documentation, statistical outputs, and figures are licensed under CC BY 4.0. The R source code is released under the MIT License.

subjects.subject: brown mushroom stem layer chicks 16S rRNA cecal microbiome RT-qPCR mucosal immunity gene expression microbiome-immune interactions Spearman correlation db-RDA neural network poultry nutrition

descriptions.description:
This dataset provides supporting data for the study “Dietary brown mushroom stem reshapes the cecal microbiome and mucosal immune response of layer chicks.”

The study evaluated dietary brown mushroom stem (BMS) across four treatment groups: Control (0% BMS), T1 (2% BMS), T2 (4% BMS), and T3 (6% BMS). Immune gene expression was measured in ileal mucosa using RT-qPCR, and the microbiome data were obtained from cecal contents.

The deposit includes technical Ct measurements, relative-expression values, sample metadata, and a data dictionary for eight immune genes: IL1B, IL6, TNF-alpha, IFN-gamma, TLR4, IL10, TGFB1, and IL4. The RT-qPCR dataset contains 40 samples, of which 39 have matching microbiome records in the supplied dataset.

Additional files include genus-level relative-abundance and count matrices, taxonomic annotations, gene–genus correlation results, distance-based redundancy analysis (db-RDA/CAP) output tables, five-fold cross-validated neural-network performance results, and the matched gene-expression matrix used for the integrated analyses. ASV-level BIOM tables, representative ASV sequences, and a QIIME2 feature-table artifact are also included.

Raw 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing reads are deposited separately in the NCBI Sequence Read Archive under BioProject accession PRJNA1504972 and are not duplicated in this deposit.

The README file describes the deposited files, treatment coding, sample matching, and data-processing information.

titles.title: VirtualFlyBrain/geppetto-vfb: v2.2.11.3 — terms come back after Clear

descriptions.description:
A term cleared from the scene can be loaded again.

Clear deletes every instance, which takes the meshes out of the scene, but the types it had resolved stay in the model. The app read that as "already loaded" — the instance is there, nothing is still an import — so asking for the term again only moved the focus to it and never put its geometry back. Once you had used Clear, those terms were dead for the rest of the session: no mesh, no Layers row, and they never returned to the i= list in the URL, so a copied link came back without them.

Reported on "Reports of transgene expression in adult mushroom body alpha'-lobe": add a few images, wait for them to load, Clear, then reopen the same query and select one again.

A term now counts as loaded only if the geometry it resolved is still in the scene. Only what the 3D viewer draws is counted, so a term whose mesh is present is loaded even if its skeleton was never shown, and a term with no geometry at all — a class with no image — behaves as before.

This one is not new: it predates the mesh work in v2.2.11.1 and v2.2.11.2, and would have affected anyone who used Clear.

The check now lives in the Focus Term test suite, where Clear itself lives. Verified on v2-dev by the reported route: five images from that query, Clear, re-select — mesh, Layers row and URL all return.

descriptions.description: Digital chromotyping is a quantitative image-based methodology for characterising the chromatic identity of fungal structures through multi-colour-space analysis of standardised digital photographs. The pileus (cap surface), hymenium (gill lamellae), and basidiospore mass (spore print) of Termitomyces manmiformis Heim — a wild edible termitophilous macrofungus from Canacona, Goa, India — were subjected to systematic digital colour analysis. Specimens were collected on 17 July 2025. Spore prints were collected on 100-micron thick Garware Polyester sheets and air-dried before photography. A vertical cross-section of the deposited spore print showing uniform basidiospore deposition was selected for colour analysis. Images were captured with a Samsung Galaxy S24 Ultra under natural light. Pixel colour data were generated using Image Colour Summarizer Version SDK33, 2024 and processed for multi-colour-space analysis across RGB, CIELAB, HSL, CMYK, XYZ, and RYB models. A total of 71 discrete named colours spanning 14 spectral groups were resolved across the three structures. The pileus showed the highest chromatic complexity (Shannon H' = 2.85; 37 named colours; 11 spectral groups), dominated by Orange-Brown tones consistent with melanin-carotenoid cuticle pigmentation. The hymenium presented a paler, near-achromatic profile (Chroma C* = 6.16; dominant colour: Ash Grey). The spore print was the most homogeneous structure (H' = 1.51; 4 spectral groups), characterised by an ochre-buff signal (L* = 66.46, b* = +24.22, C* = 24.40). Cross-structure delta-E* (CIE76) analysis showed the greatest perceptual difference between gills and spore print (delta-E* = 18.50), while pileus and spore print shared the closest chromatic centroid (delta-E* = 9.07). This study presents the first quantified digital chromotype for T. manmiformis. The author has documented approximately 35 Termitomyces taxa from Goa since 1986. A global checklist of 93 valid Termitomyces taxa accepted in MycoBank is provided.

Specimens collected from laterite scrubland habitat, Canacona taluka, South Goa, Goa, India on 17 July 2025. Colour analysis performed using Image Colour Summarizer Version SDK33, 2024 (freely accessible at http://mkweb.bcgsc.ca/color-summarizer/). The author has documented approximately 35 Termitomyces taxa from Goa, India since 1986. This is the first quantified digital chromotype for this species. The global checklist of 93 valid Termitomyces taxa (Supplementary Table S1) is included in the PDF.

titles.title: Functional Consciousness - Pillar 18: The Geometry of Consciousness

descriptions.description:
The Geometry of Consciousness: How the Mind Builds Worlds Within the World

Lilliputian hallucinations in consciousness are visions of minute people, and often minute animals, carts, or tools that fit them, set down in an ordinary room that does not itself shrink. Raoul Leroy named the syndrome in 1909 and, in 1922, already described it as a small world with internally proportionate parts, seen in relief and perspective. Blom’s 2021 review of 226 cases found the figures environmentally grounded 97% of the time, accompanied by tiny animals in 28% and by equally miniature attributes in 15%. Causes are mixed: psychiatric illness 33%, intoxications 24%, brain lesions 23%, including alcohol 19% and vision loss 12%. The phenotype is therefore a recurrent output of human vision, not the signature of one drug.
