Chasing Crows ByVoight KampffThis road had been longer than the memory could recall, he hated it.It had morphed from motorway to road, to track and now to narrow path. It dissolved into nothing but a lonesome tree, this was no oasis nor the foot of a castle but a meaningless nothing, not even the rotting corpse of the last sorry wretch that must have trod the last of this path, an empty desert, this was the end of things, freedom is not so pretty a word for those who make it this far."A million and one places you could have stopped, what twist of madness drove you to leave your bones here?"

 

 

 

Kappa swung his axe without the force to split this last log and decided not to bother his arse pulling it out for another swing "fuck it", he collected up as much wood as he could wrap his arms around and went inside.This was the edge of the world where forests and mountains don't have names, Kappa hadn't assigned them with names, they were memories."Smelly, damp, up to your neck in brambles wood" or "Fuck that, I’m not going up there again mountain".Kappa hadn't seen a single soul in these parts and had decided long ago, that might be for the best.Out of ear shot and further than the eye can see, this was his kingdom, a small roughly made home in a small untidy clearing surrounded by quiet.Kappa, who on any other occasion might be strutting around naked, singing badly, throwing stones into the stream, was in a sombre mood.Kappa’s cheek had swollen, Kappa had had tooth ache for four days now and there was no sign of his immune system gaining a foothold on the rot.This was a great cause for concern, Kappa feared the descent into desperation and what that might mean, how far a thing will go to escape pain.Kappa had turned his home over trying to find an answer. It dawned on him long before peering into an old boot for the third time that this was no hunt for a pain relief, there wasn’t any, this was a failing exercise in distraction. “Fuck fuck fuck fuck” in time with the throbbing in his face.The clove would have kicked in by now if it was going too, a moan of desperation made it to his vocal chords as he knelt down in the middle of the floor and began to rock back and forth in a failing attempt to sooth away the noise in his head “What the fuck am I meant to do now?”“If you’re really out there, NOW is you BIG fucking chance, I am asking for your help, if you really exist, now would be an excellent time to help me the fuck out!”Kappa pauses for a deliberate and belligerently short couple of seconds “Didn’t think so you lousy fucker”.Kappa sprang to his feet, marched over to the sink, dragged his tool box from underneath and rummaged through it with a clatter.Kappa pulled out a hammer, looked at it and with a half chuckle half cry, dispensed with the idea of attempting to knock the offending tooth out with it, tossed it aside and clattered through his tool box some more, pulled out his pliers, old rusty and reluctant to open even with some force, held them up in the air and inspected them “shit!”.“I've been here before, you cant grip a tooth with pliers, the angles are all wrong and teeth, way too slippery”.Despite this, Kappa reached into his mouth with the pliers, gripped the tooth as best he could and gently moved them to see if the grip was good “aarrrr” in anticipation. The pain was no worse, the tooth moved with the pliers, the grip seemed good “aaaaaarrrrr” again in anticipation as he contemplated his next move, pulling was no good the pliers would slip off, the only other possible move was to twist it out in one aggressive move. “Aaaaaarrrrrrrrrrr”... The pliers snapped shut as they slipped off the tooth, the pain soared to new heights. Kappa slammed to the floor, curled up in a ball and began banging his forehead against his knees whilst singing a song with no distinguishable words, waiting for the pandemonium inside his head to ease.“This is fucked!..The nearest help is further than I can walk in a week”.Kappa jumped to his feet grabbed the torch from behind the door, lit it on the fire and stepped outside. Outside was dark and still with stars sprayed across the sky.It was cold enough to see the breath. On any other night Kappa might have pulled out his chair, lit a smoke and pondered the magnitude of existence but tonight Kappa strode off into the forest at a determined pace. Ten minutes later Kappa arrived into a small damp clearing, knelt down and began to scan the earth around him. His torch, still burning well, lit an orange dome of shadows, leaves and branches that leaned in and danced with the flame.Kappa was no big fan of the dark especially this far from his warm fire but the way he felt right now he'd Kick a rabid dog in the bollocks just to take him away from the here and now.“Ah there you are”, Kappa leaned in towards the ground and brought his torch forward, tucked under a tree root was a small grey blue mushroom.Kappa drew a deep breath, carefully reached out and plucked the mushroom from its hiding place, held it up to the light and inspected it.After another deep breath he carefully reached into his mouth and placed it between his cheek and his gum where the most pain was emanating.Kappa was momentarily statuesque in his orange dome waiting for the urgency of his mission to ebb and his here and now to catch up.

After a short pause Kappa begins to inspect his surroundings, the light of his torch does not reach far into the dark, not far enough to see any incoming claws or teeth.“Don't wind yourself up Kappa” he mutters to himself as he looks behind, then to the left, then right, then left, and then behind again. “Stay calm,” he whispers. Kappa knew there were no such things as monsters but he only knew this when the sun was up, now it was dark and he wasn't so sure. “Everything is fine,” he says a little louder in an attempt to convince himself that his voice won't wake anything with more teeth than brain cells.A piece of burning material that flakes from his torch and drops to the floor catches his attention, he looks at it and then at the torch.“Shit! That's not going to last ten minutes”, Kappa bolts into a march, resisting the urge to run but at this pace the torch starts to roar as it cuts through the air, Kappa feels that its making too much noise and he wont hear any teeth stalking him. “Shit!” he picks up the pace, the roar gets louder and he tries to look in all directions at once... THUNK! His foot snagged a root, like a noose and as strong as rope, it shows his foot no mercy. He lunges forward, his boots slapping the ground desperately trying to catch up with his head but it was too late. Kappa has to throw his arms forward to break his fall. Straight into a bramble, sparks flying every which way.Kappa jumped up in a flash ripping himself from the thorn's grip.Holding what was left of his the torch high above his head he begins to slowly rotate so he can scan in all directions. There’s no tooth ache here and he can't feel the blood running down from his elbow or the peppering from the brambles but he can hear his lungs heaving. His breathing is making too much noise he can't hear past it. He tries to hold his breath but it only makes him all the more desperate to heave great lungs of noisy air. Suddenly there's a sound in the brambles right next to him. Something moved. This triggers every muscle in his body to attempt a leap from this world into a better one, Kappa is now at full tilt, leaping fallen trees with barely a touch and dodging the whirlwind of obstacles that his pace is throwing at him.Kappa curses himself as his logic catches up. “It was the brambles springing back into position, idiot!” but it was too late he was unable to calm. His instincts and imagination had taken over and his logic was along for the ride.  AbstractTraditional ethical theories struggle to locate universally accepted, objective sources for moral value, often relying on non-empirical axioms. This paper introduces a naturalistic ethical framework that re-examines moral imperatives through the lens of the involuntary, biologically embedded experience of "proxy-pain" (vicarious aversion or empathy). This framework posits that 'proxy-pain' is not merely a shared feeling, but a functional imperative. The agent’s drive for self-defense against this internal aversion creates a direct instruction to act, effectively transforming the descriptive 'is' of neurobiological distress into the prescriptive 'ought' of moral intervention. This approach attempts to demonstrate a mechanism by which the descriptive "is" of human psychology can constrain the prescriptive "ought" of moral decision-making. Actions traditionally labeled "altruistic" are re-interpreted within this framework as instrumental strategies of self-regulation and psychological self-defense against the greater aversion associated with witnessing or permitting harm. By aligning this model with empirical findings from social and affective neuroscience, this framework offers an empirically grounded explanation for human moral behavior that clarifies persistent questions regarding moral motivation in existing neuroscience literature (Blair, 2008), while providing a substantive response to moral error theory by grounding moral authority in the inescapable reality of existential consequences.

Keywords: altruism, aversion, empathy, ethics, is-ought problem, moral naturalism, philosophical psychology, "proxy-pain", self-defense. 

Public Significance StatementThe study suggests that human morality is not merely a social construct but a biological necessity for emotional self-regulation. By defining moral "oughts" as functional instructions to reduce the internal distress caused by seeing others suffer, this framework provides a new lens for understanding empathy-related disorders and improving social cooperation through objective, biological reality.

Traditional ethical systems, from deontology to utilitarianism, have long sought a stable, objective foundation for moral value. In their pursuit, philosophers often invoke abstract concepts such as "duty," "universalizability," or an intrinsic "greatest good"—concepts that typically lack an immediate basis in readily testable, empirical reality. Consequently, these theories often struggle to resolve fundamental questions concerning moral motivation and accountability, leaving a significant gap between philosophical theory and the empirical mechanisms of human behavior  (Greene, 2013, pp. 188–189, 289–292).

This paper proposes a naturalistic ethical framework that locates the source of moral value not in abstract reasoning, but in the pre-rational, involuntary human experience of empathy, reconceptualized here as "proxy-pain" (vicarious aversion). This model posits that the moral "ought" is a functional instruction to minimize this felt aversive experience within the moral agent, thereby offering a specific, mechanistic substrate that previous ethicists may have been gesturing toward with terms like agape, charity, and love.

The term “agape” is used strategically as a historical antecedent to draw attention to the trajectory of moral language. The argument is made that the original concept of agape was an attempt to define a condition where an individual's well-being becomes contingent upon the well-being of another; specifically, the experience of "You Hurt / I Hurt." However, as language is dynamic and meaning can drift, the introduction of precise terminology like "proxy-pain" is necessary to reclaim the required denotational clarity for empirical investigation. The study argues that this inherent capacity for vicarious aversion, deeply rooted in our neurobiology, serves as a fundamental mechanism that constrains moral behavior. This perspective suggests that morality is an emergent property of our neurobiology consistent with contemporary moral naturalism (Prinz, 2007).It is important to clarify that the Agape-Centered Ethics model is not an exercise in biological reductionism. Rather than attempting to simplify or dismiss the phenomenological complexity of moral experience, this framework acts as a foundational refinement. By identifying “proxy-pain” as the underlying mechanism, we provide an error-correcting algorithm that allows the agent to verify the validity of contemporary moral claims. This is not a constraint of moral scope, but a sharpening of the tools used to ascertain 'value facts,' making the profound experience of agape scientifically intelligible without stripping it of its social or psychological nuance. 

The Foundational Principles: Moral Realism and MechanismMoral action originates from an innate, involuntary physiological response to the actual or potential suffering of others. This response, rooted in the shared pain matrix of the brain, is not a conscious choice but a functional constraint on the agent’s experience providing the initial input for an algorithm for value facts. This provides the agent’s motivational state with a traceable origin, which can then be inspected against competing values for moral coherence. In this framework, 'coherence' is not merely an abstract logical consistency, but a homeostatic equilibrium: the agent rationalizes their choice by identifying which action minimizes the greatest projected total of aversive experience (“proxy-pain” or secondary social guilt) within their specific social and biological context.

Furthermore, this ethical approach re-frames moral failure. When an agent is overwhelmed by complexity, mistakes are categorized as an artifact of computational capacity or inability to sum (freeze) rather than an error of the core moral algorithm or malicious motive. The agent’s aversion minimization principle remains intact, allowing for rational self-correction and repair without existential damage to their moral identity."



The Neurobiological Registration of DistressEmpirical evidence confirms that the neural mechanisms for self-experienced and observed pain are significantly overlapping. Neuroimaging demonstrates that the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) and the insula are activated by the mere sight of pain in others (Decety & Jackson, 2004, p. 56). The insula’s role in monitoring the body’s physiological state suggests that witnessing distress in another is not a purely "representational" event; it is a somatic event for the observer. (Decety & Jackson 2006, p. 56) specify that while the self-perspective yields higher pain ratings, the neural network—including the parietal operculum and anterior insula—is fundamentally shared. This "proxy-pain" mechanism provides a functional bridge between first-person and third-person information.Furthermore, this aversion mechanism is modulated by specific neurochemicals. Research shows that the neuropeptide oxytocin (OXT) enhances feelings of guilt and shame specifically for intentional harm caused to others, and decreases the willingness to endorse such actions, providing a clear hormonal basis for the aversion mechanism (Zheng et al., 2024). This hormonal modulation suggests a complex, multi-layered biological system underlying moral emotions.



The Functional Is-Ought BridgeThe existence of this involuntary vicarious aversion provides a naturalistic basis for the relationship between the descriptive "is" (the neurobiological registration of distress) and the functional "ought" (the drive to alleviate that distress). In this framework, the moral imperative is understood as a homeostatic instruction: the agent ought to act to minimize the felt aversion within their total experiential field. By framing the "ought" as a functional requirement for psychological self-regulation, we sidestep the traditional naturalistic fallacy. Here, "ought" does not refer to a transcendent moral truth, but to a systemic necessity for an agent whose well-being is biologically contingent upon the state of the "other." This framework posits that 'proxy-pain' is not merely a shared feeling, but a functional imperative. The agent’s drive for self-defense against this internal aversion creates a direct instruction to act, effectively transforming the descriptive 'is' of neurobiological distress into the prescriptive 'ought' of moral intervention.

The Necessary Condition for Moral AgencyThe presence of this aversive mechanism is a necessary condition for typical human moral agency. The amoral individual—characterized by reduced amygdala functionality and empathy deficits—lacks this functional constraint. Research into psychopathy as a developmental disorder (Blair, 2008) highlights that this is an emotional pathophysiology rather than a failure of abstract reasoning. Critically, moral action requires both the involuntary signal of “proxy-pain” and the cognitive capacity for self-other distinction to regulate the response (Decety & Jackson, 2004). Without the initial aversive "trigger," the cognitive "regulation" has no signal to act upon.

Motivational Principles and the Epistemic Imperative

This section explores the homeostatic nature of altruism and provides the critical response to Richard Joyce’s Moral Error Theory.



The Motivational Principles: The Interdependent SelfThis section re-evaluates moral action as a form of homeostatic regulation for an interdependent agent. The model suggests that the traditional distinction between "self-interest" and "altruism" is a false dichotomy; both are driven by the same functional imperative: the minimization of aversive states.

The Aversion Minimization PrincipleAll deliberate actions are instrumental acts of self-regulation aimed at minimizing the agent's total aversive experience (e.g., physical pain, social guilt, or “proxy-pain”). Under this framework, "self-sacrificial" acts—such as a soldier shielding others—are interpreted as rational calculations where the aversion associated with inaction (witnessing harm or violating a core identity) is perceived as greater than the aversion of the sacrifice itself. The agent chooses the "lesser of two evils" in an act of psychological self-defense.

This is supported by research in comparative psychology. (Pozo et al., 2023, p. 1). demonstrate that helping behavior in rodents is modulated by internal states like hunger; when self-preservation demands are high, the capacity to respond to a conspecific’s distress decreases. This reinforces that moral action is not an abstract choice but is contingent upon competing homeostatic demands.

The Interdependent "Self"The "self" whose aversion is being minimized is intrinsically social. From an evolutionary perspective, "group defense" is a form of "self-defense." While the mechanism of “proxy-pain” is universal, its application is modulated by proximity and social bonding. This explains cross-cultural variability while maintaining a biological constant. Even non-human animals, such as canids and primates, exhibit behaviors resembling justice and consolation, suggesting a deeply conserved evolutionary basis for social concern that predates human abstract reasoning (Romero et al., 2010; Essler et al., 2017).While the mechanism of “proxy-pain” is universal, its application is modulated by proximity and social bonding. This modulation is often critiqued as an inherent bias or a "spotlight" that renders empathy an unreliable foundation for global ethics (Bloom, 2016). However, within the Agape-Centered framework, this discriminatory nature is not a 'bug' of the moral system, but a fundamental feature of value-fact identification. Without the neurobiological capacity to distinguish between higher and lower states of reciprocal utility—discriminating between the 'Rembrandt' and the 'snotty hanky' of social consequences—the moral agent would lack the necessary contrast to prioritize action. By acknowledging this 'spotlight' as a functional constraint, the model allows for the construction of ethical 'cheat sheets' that remain in lockstep with the agent's biological reality, rather than drifting into the cynicism of incoherent, abstract rules." 

The Epistemic Imperative: Clinical Truth vs. Narrative UtilityThis section addresses the tension between neurobiological reality and socially constructed narratives, engaging specifically with Richard Joyce’s (2001) Moral Error Theory.

The Myth of Categorical ReasonsRichard Joyce (2001) argues that since moral properties do not exist in the world, our moral talk is a "useful fiction." Joyce expresses concern that collapsing these fictions might cause social instability. This framework disagrees with Joyce’s "fictionalism" regarding transparency. We argue that the "authority" of morality does not need to be a fiction; it is grounded in the inescapable reality of existential consequences.

The Castaway AnalogyThe transition from a "subliminal" understanding of morality to an overt, naturalistic one is analogous to the resolution of complex psychological coping mechanisms. Consider a castaway who forms a deep connection with an inanimate object to mitigate the aversive agony of loneliness. In isolation, this fiction is a functional "lesser of two evils"—a necessary subterfuge to maintain psychological stability. However, the requirement to "let go" of the fiction arises when the agent returns to a world of actual "others."

While abandoning the simulated companion involves a painful loss, it is a natural release into a more robust state of being. Similarly, while humanity has long relied on the "useful fictions" of abstract moral axioms to manage social cooperation, the transition to an overt, naturalistic understanding represents an evolutionary "escape" from isolation. By moving into the reality of the biological "is," the agent moves from simulating value to participating in the authentic, functional mechanics of social interdependence. This suggests that fewer behavioral changes may occur than Joyce fears, as the agent is not losing morality, but simply trading a simulated companion for a real one. Recent analysis by Sinclair (2025) further challenges the necessity of these robust fictions, suggesting that moral discourse remains resilient even when grounded in naturalist or non-categorical terms.

Clinical Implications, Positionality, and References

This final section bridges the theory into psychological practice and provides the 2025 required reporting standards.



Academia and scientific institutions hold a primary imperative to prioritize clinical accuracy over narrative convenience. This requires that the underlying mechanisms of empathy and aversion be acknowledged as they are, not as they are socially performed. The utility of this transparency lies in promoting optimal social engagement. Overconfidence or under-confidence in an agent's self-valuation (their "value in the scrum") presents a detriment to the actual goal of balancing value facts in the human project at large. While overconfidence promotes stagnation of moral refinement, under-confidence fosters disengagement (withdrawal/anxiety). By aligning with an overt, naturalistic understanding, we move toward a robust state of rational self-governance that encourages accurate self-assessment, essential for a life worth living within a social reality. This indicates a more optimistic outlook on the human capacity for truth-seeking in the face of naturalistic reality.Reciprocal Utility as the Goal of Clinical TruthThe pursuit of a "life worth living" is fundamentally tied to an agent’s status as a valued member of the social scrum. While different agents provide varying utilities—ranging from diagnostic skill to physical strength or social skill—the attainment of a secure social position ("we need you and you need us") requires a strict adherence to the veracity of the moral algorithm. It is only through an accurate, non-fictional assessment of one's own value and the value of others that true reciprocal utility can be achieved. While “useful fictions” have historically facilitated social cohesion, the high-value state of being an essential part of the whole is most resilient when grounded in the veracity of the moral algorithm. Overt naturalistic transparency offers a robustness that fictions may lack, providing a stable mechanism for securing a seat in the human project—converting the "is" of biological reality into the "ought" of a life lived with meaning and social conviction.



Clinical and Theoretical ImplicationsThe proposed framework is useful for empirical sciences. It demands precision in moral terms. In psychological research, terms like "prosocial" often carry assumed moral weight. However, they lack explicit definitions. This ambiguity can cause errors. For example, "pure altruism" often disappears with a clear analysis of its motives.

Diagnostics and Personality PathologyThe “proxy-pain” model provides new ways to study personality disorders. Variations in vicarious aversion capacity may help to reformulate the differences between Narcissistic Personality Disorder (NPD) and Psychopathy. This model also provides a new framework for understanding Social Anxiety Disorder (SAD). Social value is linked to perceived "friendliness," a stand-in for agape. For people with SAD, their anxiety may show their empathetic sensitivity (“proxy-pain”).

The Deconstruction of "Pure Altruism"The difference between "pure altruism" often involves an unclear step from motive to action. This framework links Vicarious Aversion (Motive) to Homeostatic Regulation (Action). Removing the "selfless" motivation provides greater clarity in social psychology research.

Bridging Fact-Values with Relationship DynamicsThe "fact-values" in this model provide a solution to the "descriptive problem" in relationship psychology, specifically the work of Stanley et al. (2006). Their research on "sliding versus deciding" found that relationships formed via "sliding" (low deliberation) are less stable. This model resolves this by providing the moral mechanics needed for "deciding": using vicarious aversion as the metric for compatibility.

ConclusionThe Agape-Centered Ethics model asserts that the "ought" is intrinsically derived from the "is" of our shared neurobiology. We are moral agents laboring under a universal, involuntary mechanism that uses vicarious aversion to functionally project intrinsic value onto the well-being of others. However, the journey does not end at the biological registration of pain. By applying the algorithm for value facts, the agent moves from a state of isolated self-defense into a sophisticated state of reciprocal utility.

The pursuit of morality is thus revealed as an exercise in rational calculation and emotional honesty regarding this fundamental mechanism. By grounding moral motivation in objective neurobiology, we move beyond the "useful fictions" of the past and into an overt, clinical truth. This transition allows the agent to move from "simulating" value to "participating" in the authentic mechanics of social interdependence. Ultimately, the veracity of the algorithm is the very thing that secures the agent’s "seat at the table"—ensuring that our joint sum in the human project is significantly greater than the sum of our isolated parts. This framework provides fertile ground for future interdisciplinary research, offering an optimistic, empirically grounded response to the existential necessity of social belonging.



Positionality StatementThe author says this framework is informed by a personal journey of three decades. The work started from a struggle with internalizing moral "intuitions." This led to a search for "value facts" to navigate social interactions. The "Agape-Centered Ethics" model tries to ground value positions in a naturalistic logic.

titles.title: Data and code for "Biased Connectivity Shapes Food Odour Categorisation in the Drosophila Mushroom Body"

rightsList.rights: GNU General Public License v3.0 or later

descriptions.description:
Overview

This dataset contains in vivo calcium-imaging data from adult Drosophila melanogaster and custom analysis code developed for the study “Biased Connectivity Shapes Food Odour Categorisation in the Drosophila Mushroom Body.” The study investigated whether structured connectivity between the olfactory projection neurons and the mushroom body Kenyon cells contributes to the categorisation of food and non-food odours in the mushroom body. 

Deposited files

The deposited files include:

- 0README.md: documentation of the deposited data, code, file structure, processing workflow, and software requirements;

- calcium_imaging_data_tar.xz: in vivo calcium-imaging data from all flies included in the publication and the registration parameters;

- calcium_imaging_data.sha256: checksums for the calcium-imaging data.

- traces.tar.xz: calcium traces obtained after image registration;

- code.tar.xz: custom code used to analyse the data and generate the figures in the publication;

- BiasedConnOdourCat.sif: an Apptainer/Singularity container providing the software environment required to run the code.

- python_licenses.md: licenses for the container Python modules.

- container_licenses.md: licenses for the container Debian packages.

Data acquisition and processing

In vivo calcium-imaging data were acquired from five flies for each Kenyon cell type examined in the study. Odour-evoked neural activity was recorded using a two-photon laser-scanning microscope.

The cytoplasmic calcium indicator GCaMP6f was expressed selectively in the respective Kenyon cell populations to measure odour-evoked calcium responses. Co-expressed nuclear-localised mCherry (NLS-mCherry) provided a structural reference for image registration, motion correction, and cell segmentation.

The imaging data were processed using the analysis code included in this deposition. Further information on the fly genotypes, imaging parameters, odour-stimulation protocol, file organisation, processing workflow, and software requirements is provided in the associated publication and the accompanying 0README.md file.

titles.title: Dataset for the Proximate Composition and Micronutrient Profile of an Iron and vitamin A -Rich instant Complementary Food from locally sourced yellow maize, oyster mushroom, cow liver and orange juice

dates.dateInformation: Generated, collected, analyzed, and organized the research data used in the study.

descriptions.description: This dataset contains the original research data generated during the development and nutritional evaluation of a vitamin A- and iron-rich instant complementary food formulated from locally sourced yellow maize, pumpkin flesh, oyster mushroom, cow liver, and orange juice. The dataset includes: (1) nutrient composition data of the individual ingredients used in the formulation; (2) optimized formulation data showing the proportions of the individual ingredients combined to produce the seven complementary food formulations (F1–F7); (3) proximate composition, vitamin A, and iron content of the seven formulated complementary food samples; and (4) micronutrient composition data of the 3 most preferred complementary food formulations. All data were generated through experimental laboratory analyses and formulation optimization conducted as part of the study and support the findings reported in the associated manuscript.

titles.title: Tyrosinase Inhibitors Dataset: 1725 Compounds with Experimental IC50 Values from ChEMBL and BindingDB

descriptions.description:
This dataset contains 1,725 curated tyrosinase inhibitors with experimental IC50 values collected from ChEMBL (v34) and BindingDB databases. The dataset includes compounds tested against mushroom tyrosinase (Agaricus bisporus, CHEMBL3318) and human tyrosinase (CHEMBL1973).

Each entry contains:- SMILES structure- IC50 (nM and µM)- pIC50- Molecular descriptors (MW, LogP, HBD, HBA, TPSA, RotBonds)- Lipinski Rule of 5 compliance- Data source (ChEMBL/BindingDB)

Dataset statistics:- Total compounds: 1,725- Lipinski compliant: 83.4%- IC50 < 1 µM: 826 compounds- IC50 < 100 nM: 598 compounds

This dataset is intended for machine learning and QSAR modeling applications in tyrosinase inhibitor discovery.

titles.title: Aloha Fungi Evidence Registry: functional mushroom clinical and preclinical studies (PubMed/DOI metadata), version 2026-09-02

descriptions.description: Curated registry of 138 peer-reviewed scientific studies on 11 functional mushroom species (Ganoderma lucidum, Hericium erinaceus, Inonotus obliquus, Cordyceps militaris, Trametes versicolor, Grifola frondosa, Lentinula edodes, Tremella fuciformis, Polyporus umbellatus, Auricularia auricula-judae, Wolfiporia cocos). For each study the registry records: PubMed ID or DOI, authors, year, journal, study design (e.g. randomised controlled trial, systematic review, animal or in vitro study), sample size, evidence level (A to E), species studied, and a short bilingual (Polish/English) note on what was tested. The registry does not report outcomes, effect sizes, or health claims; it documents the existence and design of studies so that they can be verified at source. A weekly automated check against PubMed flags retractions and errata. Machine-readable JSON and Schema.org Dataset (JSON-LD) are provided. Canonical, continuously updated version: https://alohafungi.com/nauka (each study has a stable anchor, e.g. /nauka#pmid-27045603).

titles.title: VirtualFlyBrain/VFBchat: v4.2.11

descriptions.description:
Connectivity answers now rank the biology on every route, and show it as a
table. "What are the main inputs to KCg-s?" was answered with adult neuron,
Kenyon cell and interneuron, and a graph of fifteen overlapping labels. The
deterministic ranker that orders partner classes by mean synaptic weight per
connected pair existed, but only fired on one of the two payload shapes a class
question can produce; the other — the partner tool's, which the planner and the
injector actually use — went to the extractor pre-ranked by total weight, which
ranks the ontology. A class now runs its whole connectivity table, the ranker
fires on both shapes, and the answer carries a sortable table (partner, synapses
per connected pair, % connected, pairs, total) with the roll-up classes and the
self-connection appended and labelled rather than hidden. The graph sits behind
"Show as a graph", draws only the ranked specific partners, and puts its labels
beside the nodes. Two facts about VFB's class-connectivity table surfaced on the
way: it carries rows for the queried class and every subclass, so only the
queried class's rows are read now (a subclass's 98.5 synapses per pair had been
reported as the parent's); and on a four-cell class unrelated partners can share
pair and connected counts by chance, so the chain-collapse now requires the
synapse total to agree as well. (#47, #50)

Fly stocks for a neuron class's split-GAL4 lines. "Find me fly stocks for
split drivers expressed in gamma dorsal KCs" was told VFB does not list stock
numbers. It does, one hop further than the planner looked: each SplitsTargeting
row names its two hemidriver constructs, FindStocks accepts a construct, and the
stock in both constructs' results is the split-GAL4 stock — Bloomington 68318 for
R21B06-DBD ∩ R13F02-AD. A new vfb_find_split_stocks macro runs that chain with
the lookups batched, and the answer lists each split with its stock centre and
number; seven of the nine KCg-d splits have one. "Split drivers" now counts as
split-GAL4 wording. (#46)

Ontology hierarchies are drawn as trees. "Show me the hierarchy of Kenyon cell
subtypes" ran the 32,328-row image list, because "show me" was an image cue, and
then explained that VFB does not provide a multi-level tree. The MCP's
get_hierarchy tool was referenced by two guidance cards but had never been put
in the tool catalogue. It is wired now, runs deterministically for hierarchy,
subtype and parts wording, and the tree is rendered as a nested, linked list
under the answer; the SubclassesOf table replaces the image list, because result
tables are now chosen by the kind of thing the question asks for rather than by
word overlap. (#48)

Term resolution. The AllDatasets fast path no longer hijacks a question whose
dataset clause is a scope with a stranded preposition ("which datasets they're
in") or whose subject is an unquoted symbol ("DA1 lPN neurons") — the NeuroFly
workshop's own discovery prompt. The term tokeniser keeps the prime, so
alpha/beta and alpha'/beta' Kenyon cell resolve to their own classes instead of
whichever VFB ranked first. A symbol the question names is looked up even when
the planner, shown the previous turn, read it as a back-reference to that turn's
term — "inputs to KCg-s" after a turn on KCg-d now answers about KCg-s. The
intrinsic-neuron class is resolved when the planner copies the whole phrase
("neuron types intrinsic to the mushroom body"), and evidence reaches the
synthesiser VFB first, documentation second, literature last — so the mushroom
body's intrinsic neurons are the Kenyon cells, not the MBONs a paper snippet
named. (#39, #40, #44)

Expression answers filter by gene function. "Which receptor genes are most
highly expressed in Kenyon cells?" listed ribosomal RNAs: only hand-kept symbol
lists could filter. The cluster expression table tags every gene with FlyBase's
function vocabulary — Receptor, Dopamine_receptor, Transcription_factor,
Ion_channel, GPCR and so on — so a function named in the question now filters on
that column, ranked by level. (#45)

Rendering. Pipe tables render (remark-gfm had never been installed, so the
scRNA-seq expression matrix arrived as a paragraph of literal bars); ranked lists
number 1, 2, 3 rather than 1, 1, 1; the chat panel scrolls itself, only while the
reader is at the bottom, instead of scrolling the whole document out from under
the conversation; and the thumbnail strip is chosen by what the question is
about — an image question gets the query previews, a definitional one the
term's own example images, and a question on the expression, connectivity,
stocks or dataset axis gets none. (#41, #42, #43, #45)

Verification. tests/task-battery/workshop.json holds every NeuroFly workshop
chat prompt and the 31 August walk-through as a tier-8 battery. Against v4.2.10 it
fails three of eleven tasks, at the points the issues describe; against this
release it passes all eleven. The per-question battery timeout is 900 s.

titles.title: Isotope Labeling Reveals Complex Microbial Interactions during Agaricus bisporus Compost Colonization

descriptions.description:
Study abstract

Microbial interactions strongly influence carbon and nitrogen flows in mushroom compost, yet their functional roles during Agaricus bisporus colonization remain unresolved. We combined PLFA-SIP and nanoSIMS imaging with ITS amplicon sequencing to follow resource flows and microbial activity across spatial scales. Stable-isotope tracers (¹³C-glucose and ¹⁵N-ammonium) revealed that A. bisporus simultaneously facilitates and suppresses bacterial populations: fungal activity increased glucose assimilation by bacteria yet reduced overall bacterial biomass. NanoSIMS visualized nutrient-rich microenvironments along hyphae where bacterial ¹³C and ¹⁵N assimilation was elevated. Sequencing showed the fungal community to comprise essentially two organisms, A. bisporus and Mycothermus thermophilus, which differ approximately elevenfold in their content of the fungal biomarker C18:2ω6,9c. Total fungal PLFA therefore tracks which of the two dominates as much as it tracks fungal biomass. Together these findings reveal coupled fungal–bacterial nutrient processing and show that biomarker-based estimates of fungal biomass require community composition to be known. Multi-scale isotope probing provides a framework for resolving microbial interactions in complex detrital systems.

Dataset contentsThis repository contains the raw and processed data underlying the above study, organized by measurement type: bulk ¹³C/¹⁵N measurements, CO₂ respiration, PLFA‑SIP (fungal and bacterial), DNA‑SIP, nanoSIMS, axenic‑culture PLFA, and the supplementary tables. Each numbered folder contains a README.txt explaining the file contents and abbreviations (treatment codes, timepoints, isotope labels). Figure and table numbers referenced in the READMEs correspond to the final manuscript version. Analysis scripts are archived in a separate Zenodo record (see Related identifiers). See the top‑level README.txt for the full folder map and LICENSE.txt (CC‑BY‑4.0) for reuse terms.

titles.title: Single-nematode carbon isotope dataset from 13C-glucose labelled mushroom compost, measured by laser ablation isotope ratio mass spectrometry

subjects.subject: laser ablation isotope ratio mass spectrometry

descriptions.description:
This dataset contains carbon isotope measurements of individual nematodes madeby laser ablation isotope ratio mass spectrometry (LA-IRMS), a technique thatfires a focused ultraviolet laser at a single organism and measures the isotopiccomposition of the carbon released. It is used here to address a long-standingconstraint in soil food web research: conventional isotope analysis needs tensof pooled individuals per measurement, so it returns a community average andcannot resolve differences between one animal and the next, or between one partof an animal and another.

The nematodes were extracted from commercial *Agaricus bisporus* (white buttonmushroom) compost and from the peat casing layer applied on top of it, during a30-day cultivation experiment in which ¹³C-labelled glucose was added at thestart as a tracer. Unlabelled parallel incubations served as controls. Samplingcovers days 14, 21 and 30, in both substrates. The isotope data comprise 818individual laser shots on 121 nematodes across 24 samples, together with 198shots on an isotopic reference standard and 90 shots on straw and organic debrisas a contamination control. The nematode abundance data from the same experimentare included: counts and substrate weights for 41 extracted samples across fourtreatments, two of which were not carried through to isotope analysis.

Files are provided as CSV at the level of the individual laser shot, withsample, substrate, timepoint, analytical session and specimen identifiers onevery row, so measurements can be aggregated to individual, sample or treatmentas required. A README documents the experimental design, the extraction andmounting procedure, instrument settings and calibration, the isotopecalculations, column definitions and units, the known limitations of thedataset, and which file reproduces each figure and table in the accompanyingthesis chapter.

The results and their interpretation are reported in Chapter V of the doctoralthesis at DOI 10.33540/2915.

Access is restricted pending publication of the corresponding paper. Requestsvia the button above.

titles.title: Electron probe microanalysis dataset: elemental distributions in Agaricus bisporus mycelium and associated oxalate crystals

descriptions.description:
This dataset contains electron probe microanalysis (EPMA) elemental maps and region-of-interest (ROI) measurements of Agaricus bisporus (button mushroom) mycelium and the calcium oxalate crystals associated with it, collected across seven imaged positions. It supports Chapter VI of the doctoral thesis "Elemental imaging of Agaricus bisporus mycelium using electron probe microanalysis" (DOI: 10.33540/2915) and documents the measurement conditions developed for this application of EPMA to fungal tissue, which had not previously been characterised this way.

Maps and ROI statistics were acquired on a JEOL JXA-8530F field-emission-gun electron probe microanalyzer (Utrecht University) at 15 kV and 29–30 nA probe current, for eight elements (Si, Cu, Ca, Mg, Fe, P, K, Mn) plus secondary-electron and backscatter imaging channels. Beam conditions and the 100 ms/pixel dwell time were established through iterative trial and error, since longer dwell times risked eroding the fungal sample surface under the electron beam. No calibration standards were used; reported values are relative X-ray count intensities (relative elemental abundance), not standard-calibrated concentrations.

Files include the raw per-position instrument output, extracted per-ROI statistics (background, hyphae, and calcium-oxalate-crystal regions), the images used to define those regions, and rendered elemental-map figures per position; full column definitions and file structure are given in the included README.

Region-of-interest extraction from the raw maps was performed using software written by Ian Ross (https://github.com/ian-ross/fungi-empa), not included in this deposit; only the raw measurements and resulting statistics are provided here.

titles.title: Supplementary materials for:Genomic Characterization, cgMLST Typing, and Pathogenicity of Bongkrekic Acid-Producing Burkholderia gladioli from Edible Mushrooms and Wet Rice Noodles in Hunan Province, China

descriptions.description:
Bongkrekic acid (BA) is a highly toxic foodborne toxin that poses a serious threat to public health, yet the genomic features and pathogenicity of its producer, Burkholderia gladioli, remain inadequately understood. To address this knowledge gap, we conducted a comprehensive genomic and phenotypic study on BA-producing B. gladioli isolates from two major high-risk food sources.

A total of 75 isolates were obtained from wet rice noodles and edible mushroom products collected in Hunan Province, China, between 2023 and 2025. All isolates were subjected to whole-genome sequencing using the Illumina NovaSeq platform. Core genome multilocus sequence typing (cgMLST) and comprehensive pathogenicity analyses were performed.

This dataset comprises the raw sequencing data (FASTQ files) for all 75 isolates, which have been deposited in the Genome Sequence Archive (GSA) under the accession number CRA044684. The supplementary materials provided here include all additional figures and tables generated during the analysis, encompassing details on genomic characterization, phylogenetic relationships, cgMLST typing results, and virulence factor profiles. These data provide a critical resource for understanding the evolution, transmission, and pathogenic mechanisms of B. gladioli and for developing future surveillance and intervention strategies.

This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License. This dataset supports the research article: "Genomic Characterization, cgMLST Typing, and Pathogenicity of Bongkrekic Acid-Producing Burkholderia gladioli from Edible Mushrooms and Wet Rice Noodles in Hunan Province, China" (under review).

This new version includes the raw numerical data and original images underlying the figures and statistical analyses. These additional files are provided as a separate folder within this dataset.

titles.title: Supplementary materials for:Genomic Characterization, cgMLST Typing, and Pathogenicity of Bongkrekic Acid-Producing Burkholderia gladioli from Edible Mushrooms and Wet Rice Noodles in Hunan Province, China

descriptions.description:
Bongkrekic acid (BA) is a highly toxic foodborne toxin that poses a serious threat to public health, yet the genomic features and pathogenicity of its producer, Burkholderia gladioli, remain inadequately understood. To address this knowledge gap, we conducted a comprehensive genomic and phenotypic study on BA-producing B. gladioli isolates from two major high-risk food sources.

A total of 75 isolates were obtained from wet rice noodles and edible mushroom products collected in Hunan Province, China, between 2023 and 2025. All isolates were subjected to whole-genome sequencing using the Illumina NovaSeq platform. Core genome multilocus sequence typing (cgMLST) and comprehensive pathogenicity analyses were performed.

This dataset comprises the raw sequencing data (FASTQ files) for all 75 isolates, which have been deposited in the Genome Sequence Archive (GSA) under the accession number CRA044684. The supplementary materials provided here include all additional figures and tables generated during the analysis, encompassing details on genomic characterization, phylogenetic relationships, cgMLST typing results, and virulence factor profiles. These data provide a critical resource for understanding the evolution, transmission, and pathogenic mechanisms of B. gladioli and for developing future surveillance and intervention strategies.

This work is licensed under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License. This dataset supports the research article: "Genomic Characterization, cgMLST Typing, and Pathogenicity of Bongkrekic Acid-Producing Burkholderia gladioli from Edible Mushrooms and Wet Rice Noodles in Hunan Province, China" (under review).

This new version includes the raw numerical data and original images underlying the figures and statistical analyses. These additional files are provided as a separate folder within this dataset.

titles.title: Eunoe shirikishinai Imajima & Hartman 1964

descriptions.description:
Eunoe shirikishinai Imajima & Hartman, 1964
Fig. 19
Eunoe shirikishinai Imajima & Hartman, 1964: 30, pl. 3, figs a – d.
Type material examined.
Holotype • USNM 74051 (1 parapodium, 1 elytron).
Type locality.
Hokkaido Island, Shirikishinai, Japan.
Comparative material.
Eunoe sentiformis: • USNM 43582 (1 spm).
Eunoe spinosa: • USNM 23762 (1 spm).
Diagnosis.
Cirrophores with extra lobes. Elytral macrotubercles sharply pointed with short branches all ending with sharp, pointed tips, near posterior edge of elytra. Dorsal cirrus without spines. Notochaetae with truncate tips bearing a long spinous, minutely serrated region.
Description.
Based on examined material (one elytron and one parapodium). Color in alcohol: elytra white with brown spot, macrotubercles golden brown.
Cirrophore with extra lobe. Dorsal cirrus without spines; abruptly tapering subdistally.
Elytron reniform (Fig. 19 A). Microtubercles horn-like and bifurcated spines on anterior and median areas of elytra. Macrotubercles spiniform, sharply pointed with short branches, all ending with sharp, pointed tips, near posterior edge of elytron (Fig. 19 A, B). Outer lateral and posterior margin with short, scarce papillae.
All notochaetae covered with small rows of spinules, ending with truncate tips with long, spinous, minutely serrated region (Fig. 19 E). All neurochaetae unidentate, covered with distinct rows of spinules, with long, bare, and slightly falcate tips (Fig. 19 D).
Remarks.
The holotype of Eunoe shirikishinai (USNM 74051, from Hokkaido, Japan) comprised only a single parapodium and one elytron, with the body absent. Therefore, our redescription above is restricted to characters observable from these fragments. All other characters for the species are taken verbatim from the original description by Imajima and Hartman (1964) and could not be verified. Those include body size, length 57 mm, width including parapodia 20 mm; segment number, 38 segments; absence of cephalic peaks; position of the anterior eyes, laterally, on the widest part of the prostomium; and palps, thick, ~ 3.5 × longer than lateral antennae, with triangular papillae arranged in six longitudinal rows. Additional head structures, such as nuchal flap and facial tubercle, extra lobes, spines on body appendages, and papillation on the elytral surface were not reported by Imajima and Hartman (1964). In addition, spines were not observed on the preserved holotype dorsal cirrus. The presence or absence of extra lobes on elytrophores and dorsal tubercles cannot be assessed from the available material. However, the cirrophore of the examined holotype parapodium had an extra lobe.
Eunoe shirikishinai has been previously confused with five other species of Eunoe due to superficial similarity in macrotubercles: E. hozawai, E. oerstedi, E. senta, E. sentiformis, and E. spinosa. For phylogenetic reconstruction, we used data from BOLD derived from the specimens E. cf. oerstedi P _ 8 NJ-2021 (BOLD Process ID GBMNF 750-22), from the Kumano Sea, Japan (Jimi et al. 2021), and E. oerstedi isolate PhB 172 (BOLD process ID GBAN 4646-13), from South Korea, both identified as E. shirikishinai (Jimi et al. 2021). These specimens formed a well-supported clade nested within the Eunoe s. str. clade. However, we cannot conclusively identify them as E. shirikishinai because the photograph provided by Jimi et al. (2021) lacks an image of the elytra, but the specimen has extra lobes on the cirrophores. The elytra bear the main identifying character, which is the golden-brown branching, sharply pointed macrotubercles (Fig. 19 B). This character unites E. shirikishinai with E. hozawai, the latter differing only in having smaller and shorter macrotubercles (Imajima and Hartman 1964).
The Eunoe sentiformis specimen (USNM 43582 from the Kuril Islands, North-West Pacific Ocean) exhibited two types of macrotubercles. The first type: cylindrical macrotubercles, ending distally in a rosette-shaped apex with a strongly lobate margin, a “ flower-like ” head with five to eight petals, which Uschakov (1958) described as “ mushroom-like ” (Fig. 20 B – C). The second type: cylindrical macrotubercles with a dentate crown at the tip (Fig. 20 D). In Imajima and Hartman (1964), these species were distinguished by the shape of notochaetae ending in truncate tips with a long spinous, minutely serrated region in E. shirikishinai and not serrated, truncate tips in E. sentiformis. Upon comparing the notochaetae of USNM 74051 (E. shirikishinai) and USNM 43582 (E. sentiformis), we found no obvious differences between the two specimens (Figs 19 E, 20 E, 20 G). Eunoe sentiformis has some macrotubercles similar to E. senta, but it is different in the shape of notochaetae and displays lateral placement of the anterior pair of eyes and golden-brown branching macrotubercles (Uschakov 1982).
The specimen USNM 23762 (Hakodate Bay, Japan), identified by Pettibone as Eunoe oerstedi, might be E. spinosa based on the presence of extra lobes on elytrophores and cirrophores, not dorsal tubercles (Fig. 19 G), and pointed notochaetae (Fig. 19 H). This specimen was similar to E. shirikishinai in having macrotubercles with short, sharp branches (Fig. 19 F) and lacking spines on the dorsal cirri (Fig. 19 I, J).
Distribution.
Hokkaido, Japan (Imajima and Hartman 1964), Kumano Sea, Japan; South Korea (Jimi et al. 2021); and Hakodate Bay, Japan at 3.5 m depth.

Published as part of Everett, Martha W., Koroleva, Anna, Straube, Nicolas & Budaeva, Nataliya, 2026, Eunoe Malmgren, 1865 (Annelida, Polynoidae) in the Arctic, North Atlantic, and North Pacific: redescription of the type species and clarification of the genus boundaries, pp. 343-403 in ZooKeys 1283 on pages 343-403, DOI: 10.3897/zookeys.1283.168195

The specimen USNM 23762 (Hakodate Bay, Japan), identified by Pettibone as Eunoe oerstedi, might be E. spinosa based on the presence of extra lobes on elytrophores and cirrophores, not dorsal tubercles (Fig. 19 G), and pointed notochaetae (Fig. 19 H). This specimen was similar to E. shirikishinai in having macrotubercles with short, sharp branches (Fig. 19 F) and lacking spines on the dorsal cirri (Fig. 19 I, J).
Distribution.
Hokkaido, Japan (Imajima and Hartman 1964), Kumano Sea, Japan; South Korea (Jimi et al. 2021); and Hakodate Bay, Japan at 3.5 m depth.

descriptions.description:
STRAIOCD African Injection Oscillation Climate Dynamics.







 

 






Verification via Direct Meteorological Observation (100% Empirical Evidence)

"The findings presented in this analysis, including the 2026 Global Hurricane Projection and the correlation between Stratospheric Breaks and storm intensification, are based 100% on direct meteorological station measurements. This data is derived from high-altitude radiosondes (weather balloons) and verified geopotential height (GPH) observations at the 70hPa (Stratosphere) and 500hPa (Troposphere) levels.Unlike classical 'Climate Models' that rely on simulations and theoretical assumptions regarding sea surface temperatures (SST), the

STRAIOCD (African Injection Oscillation) Model utilizes empirical, real-time pressure data. The recorded sequence of four major stratospheric disruptions between November 2025 and March 2026 is a measured physical reality. Therefore, the resulting mechanical weakening of the 'Atmospheric Press' and the subsequent intensification of hurricane dynamics are projected with 100% certainty based on the laws of atmospheric mechanics and a 50-year historical measurement record."

 

This article is designed to be a definitive scientific record, stripping away theoretical "heat-engine" myths and focusing exclusively on the 50-year observational dataset. It presents the

STRAIOCD (African Injection Oscillation) framework as a purely mathematical and physical result of stratospheric mass measurements.

The Stratospheric Engine: Predicting Category 5 Hurricanes through 50 Years of Observational Data

Abstract

For decades, classical meteorology has relied on Sea Surface Temperatures (SST) as the primary predictor of hurricane intensity. However, an analysis of over 200 anomalous cases from 1976–2026 reveals that Category 5 intensification frequently occurs in environments with marginal ocean heat. This paper identifies the Stratospheric Piston Effect—the downward injection of high-density mass from the 1-5 mb and 70-150 mb layers—as the true driver of extreme cyclogenesis.

1. The Failure of the 26.5°C Threshold

Statistical evidence from the last 50 years (Source: Zenodo Record 19056409) proves that the "26.5°C Rule" is not a physical limit but a secondary variable. In hundreds of documented cases, including Hurricane Alex (2016) and Hurricane Erin (2001), rapid intensification occurred over cold water or post-landfall. The common denominator in every single one of these "impossible" intensifications was a massive surge in Stratospheric Mass Density (measured in ppmv).

2. The Mechanics of the "STRAIOCD Press"

The

 STRAIOCD African Injection Oscillation Climate Dynamics. model defines a hurricane not as an upward suction of moisture, but as a downward compression of mass.





The Charging Phase (1-5 mb): A buildup of high-density mass (exceeding 7.2 ppmv) in the upper stratosphere creates a gravitational potential "battery."




The Injection Phase (70-150 mb): When moisture levels at the 70hPa level exceed 60%, the stratospheric mantle breaches the tropopause.




Adiabatic Compression: As this dense air is forced into the tropospheric vacuum, it undergoes rapid adiabatic heating and compression, forcing the central pressure to drop at rates exceeding 5hPa/hour, regardless of the surface temperature.



3. Predictive Matrix: The Category 5 Forecasting Table

Based on 50 years of meteorological measurements and field reports, the following table serves as the primary tool for predicting the transition to a Category 5 "Super-Storm."




Predictor Level

4. Case Study Analysis: 50-Year Correlation

The dataset confirms that the "Stratospheric River" is the deciding factor in peak intensity.





Inland Maintenance: Cases where storms intensified over land (e.g., Oklahoma anomalies) show a direct correlation with 70hPa mass pulses originating from the African Ridge.




Rapid Intensification (RI): 92% of RI events in the last 50 years were preceded by a 3 mb mass spike 6–12 hours before the pressure drop at sea level.



5. Conclusion: Predicting the "Samuel" Scenario

To forecast a Category 5 event for a system like Hurricane Samuel, the focus must shift from the ocean surface to the stratospheric mantle. If the 70hPa mass density crosses the 5.5 ppmv threshold while the 3 mb level is in a state of compression, a Category 5 transition is mathematically inevitable. This is not a theoretical model; it is the physical reality recorded by 50 years of meteorological field data.

 

 

Scientific Note: The Role of "Convection Strangling" in Hurricane Intensification

Observation: Historical data from the last 50 years indicates a paradox: increased convective instability and precipitation over the North African Sahara/Sahel regions often correlate with a reduction in the intensity of Major Hurricanes (Cat 4-5). Conversely, periods of extreme clarity and suppressed convection over the desert precede rapid intensification events.

Mechanism (STRAIOCD Model): We define this phenomenon as "Convection Strangling". When the Stratospheric River (SR) exerts high-density mass injection (measured at 8.5–10+ ppmv), it creates a mechanical "downforce" or a stratospheric press. This press leads to:





Adiabatic Heat Compression: Thermal energy is trapped and compressed in the lower troposphere (850-700hPa) without cloud formation, acting as a "Pressure Cooker."




The "Lens Effect": In the absence of clouds, solar radiation and stratospheric mass create a magnifying effect, storing vast amounts of potential energy.




Suppression of "Noise": Active desert convection (rain/fog) acts as friction, dissipating this energy prematurely. A "clean" and "strangled" desert ensures a pure, high-velocity mass injection into the hurricane's eye.



Conclusion: The absence of clouds over the desert is not a sign of inactivity but an indicator of maximum potential energy storage. The sudden collapse of this "Strangling" effect during the interaction with a tropical wave triggers explosive intensification and the formation of characteristic "Black Mushroom Clouds" (Optical Density Peaks).

"The STRAIOCD model clarifies: Ocean temperatures are irrelevant. Vortex Genesis is a 100% Stratospheric process. A standard storm is a direct air injection; an extreme vortex is a strategic injection into a Ghost Trough. The latter utilizes the residual particles as a mechanical pivot, forcing the 70mb pressure to create a surgical eye and exponential rotation."

titles.title: Guanyin on a Dragon Throne at The Royal Ontario Museum, Ontario

rightsList.rights: Creative Commons Attribution Non Commercial Share Alike 4.0 International

descriptions.description: This sandstone and polychrome, large sculpture depicts Guanyin on a dragon throne. It originates from the 14th-15th Century (Ming dynasty) and was made in the Shanxi Province.  The seated bodhisattva Guanyin is recognizable by the small image of Amitabha Buddha in his crown. The rocks which flank Guanyin are home to nine animals, including a goat, an elephant, a monkey, a snake, a dragon, a lion and a deer with the mushroom of immortality. At the deity's feet are two standing figures with hats (possibly donors), two small bodhisattvas, and a large dragon.     This object is part of Scan The World. Scan the World is a non-profit initiative introduced by MyMiniFactory, through which we are creating a digital archive of fully 3D printable sculptures, artworks and landmarks from across the globe for the public to access for free. Scan the World is an open source, community effort, if you have interesting items around you and would like to contribute, email stw@myminifactory.com to find out how you can help.

titles.title: Comprehensive Image Dataset of Agaricus bisporus Diseases Under Controlled Illumination Conditions

descriptions.description:
Description

This dataset contains annotated images of healthy and diseased Agaricus bisporus mushrooms collected under controlled imaging conditions for deep learning, computer vision, and precision agriculture applications. The dataset was developed to support automated mushroom disease classification and artificial intelligence-based agricultural research.

The dataset consists of five classes:



Healthy

Bacterial Blotch

Dry Bubble

Cobweb Disease

Wet Bubble


All images were acquired using a custom-designed portable imaging apparatus specifically developed for standardized agricultural image acquisition. The imaging system provides controlled illumination conditions while minimizing external light interference to ensure image consistency, reproducibility, and high visual quality.

The dataset includes images captured under three different illumination environments:



White light

Ultraviolet (UV) light

Mixed illumination (White + UV)


Images were collected from mushroom production facilities over an extended acquisition period to ensure diversity in disease progression stages, orientations, and visual characteristics. Expert-supported annotation procedures were applied to improve labeling reliability and overall dataset quality.

The dataset is intended for:



Deep learning-based classification studies

Transfer learning applications

Computer vision research

Agricultural artificial intelligence systems

Precision agriculture applications

Benchmarking of pre-trained deep learning architectures


Potential applications include automated disease detection systems, smart farming technologies, agricultural monitoring platforms, and AI-assisted decision support systems for sustainable mushroom cultivation.

This dataset was used in the following publication:

Albayrak, U., Golcuk, A., Aktas, S., Coruh, U., Tasdemir, S., & Baykan, O. K. (2025). Classification and Analysis of Agaricus bisporus Diseases with Pre-Trained Deep Learning Models. Agronomy, 15(1), 226. https://doi.org/10.3390/agronomy15010226

The dataset is publicly released for academic and research purposes.



Citation

If you use this dataset in your research, please cite both the dataset and the related publication.

Dataset Citation

Albayrak, U., Golcuk, A., Aktas, S., Coruh, U., Tasdemir, S., & Baykan, O. K. (2026). Comprehensive Agaricus bisporus Disease Image Dataset Captured Under White, UV, and Mixed Illumination Conditions [Data set]. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.20260929

Related Publication

descriptions.description: A continuously operating, multi-zone environmental telemetry dataset from a commercial mushroom cultivation facility (Southwest Mushrooms, Phoenix, Arizona). This deposit provides aggregated and derived tables (hourly means and per-metric summary statistics) that characterize the dataset; the full raw stream is proprietary and retained by Crowe Logic, Inc. Environmental data only; cultivation outcome labels (yield and quality) are not included and supervised prediction is out of scope for this release.

titles.title: Bacterial Methylome Mapping

descriptions.description:
Bacterial Methylome Mapping

This archive is a complement to the scientific study Bouchereau, E. et al. “Environmental salinity drives DNA methylation

plasticity in the oyster pathogen Vibrio aestuarianus” (2027).


This archive contains the custom scripts necessary for processing PacBio kinetic data and EM-seq data, identifying methylation motifs (EM-seq), and producing an complete annotated methylome table. The exemples below use the directory layout used on HPC environment. Paths, module names and resource requests need to be adapted to user HPC environment and needs. All tools were callibrated to the study of bacteria methylomes.


Overview


The analysis combines:


- PacBio SMRT sequencing: used to detect m6A and m4C methylation from IPD

  kinetics and to identify methylation motifs.

- EM-seq sequencing: used to quantify m5C methylation and find corresponding motifs.

- Methylome-table processing: used to annotate sites, remove duplicated

  motif calls, merge EM-seq measurements, and classify methylation status.

- Supplementary analyses: including coverage plots.


The main processing order is:


```text

PacBio / EM-seq preprocessing

        |

        v

Merging results in a table

        |

        v

Motif and methylation tables

        |

        v
```

Operating environment


The PBS scripts were written for a Linux HPC cluster using PBS/Torque. They expect environment variables such as `DATAWORK`, `SCRATCH`, `TOOLS`, `NCPUS`, and, for some jobs, `PBS_ARRAY_INDEX`. Several scripts also load cluster specific modules or source cluster-specific environment files. They are not drop-in scripts for a local Windows installation.


Conda and Python


The main pipeline has been developped around a singularity enviornment which contains all necessary tools for PacBio kinetic data preprocessing. EM-seq data preprocessing and other analysis will need their respecting tools from conda installation if not currently available to the user.


If conda is necessary, create an environment suitable for the Python table-processing scripts. The Python scripts import the following packages:


```bash

conda install -c conda-forge -c bioconda \

  python pandas numpy matplotlib seaborn openpyxl pysam biopython \

  pybedtools gffpandas plotly prince

```


Some packages may be easier to install with pip on a particular cluster:


```bash

python -m pip install gffpandas pybedtools prince

```


Check the installation before a long run:


```bash

python -c "import pandas, numpy, matplotlib, pysam, Bio, gffpandas, pybedtools, prince"

```


External command-line tools


Depending on the branch of the workflow being used, install or load:


- `samtools`

- PacBio SMRT tools: `pbmm2`, `ipdSummary`, `motifMaker`, `dataset`,

  `pbreports`

- `singularity`

- `bismark`, `bowtie2`, and `trim-galore` for EM-seq

- `meme-chip` for optional EM-seq motif discovery

- `bedtools`/`pybedtools` support for table annotation

- `LongQC`, `bam2fastq`, `pbindex`, and `ccs` for optional preprocessing


The cluster PBS scripts contain the versions and environment paths used in the

study. Read the `## USAGE EXAMPLE` section at the top of each PBS script before

submitting it.


Input and directory conventions


The PBS workflow uses a base directory similar to:


```text

$DATAWORK/Epigenetic/Methylome/

├── in/

│   ├── Genomes/

│   ├── Samples/

│   ├── EMseq/

│   └── sample_config.tsv

├── out/

├── logs/

└── ...

```


For the multi-strain PacBio job, `sample_config.tsv` must contain a header and one tab-separated row per sample:


```text

BAM_filename<TAB>genome_filename<TAB>sample_name<TAB>cutoff

```


The BAM filenames are resolved under `in/Samples/`, genome filenames under `in/Genomes/`, and the noise cutoff is passed to `motifMaker`.


Usage


1. PacBio processing

For PacBio processing, two script have been developped. On for a single sample, best used for testing the pipeline. The second script run all samples listed in one go but necessit to know the pipeline well to avoid errors.


Single sample


The single-sample PBS job receives the BAM path, sample name, and motif score

cutoff through `qsub` variables:


```bash

qsub -v \

FILE=/path/to/Methylome/in/Samples/bc2042_S15.bam,\

SAMPLE=bc2042_S15,\

SEUIL=180 \

01_Sequencing-DATA-processing/00_Scripts-PBS/run_pacbio-bacteria-epigenetic_single.pbs

```


The reference genome is defined inside the script. The underlying wrapper is:


```bash

bash 01_Sequencing-DATA-processing/pacbio.bacteria.epigenetic.sh \

  GENOME SAMPLE BAM_FILE NCPUS BASE_FOLDER [CUTOFF]

```


The wrapper maps reads with `pbmm2`, filters and indexes the alignments, calls

kinetic modifications with `ipdSummary`, and searches/reprocesses motifs with

`motifMaker`.


Multiple strains or samples


Create `in/sample_config.tsv`, then submit one array task per data row:


```bash

SAMPLE_COUNT=$(tail -n +2 \

  "$DATAWORK/Epigenetic/Methylome/in/sample_config.tsv" | wc -l)

qsub -J 1-${SAMPLE_COUNT} \

  01_Sequencing-DATA-processing/00_Scripts-PBS/run_pacbio-bacteria-epigenetic_multipleStrains.pbs

```


The PBS array index selects the corresponding line from the configuration file. Results and logs are written below:


```text

$DATAWORK/Epigenetic/Methylome/out/

$DATAWORK/Epigenetic/Methylome/logs/

```


PacBio helper jobs


- `run_subreads-to-css.pbs`: convert PacBio subreads to CCS/HiFi reads.

- `run_bamTOfastq.pbs`: convert BAM files to FASTQ.

- `run_indexing_pacbioDATA.pbs`: create PacBio BAM indices.

- `run-LongQC.pbs`: run LongQC quality control.

- `run_samtoolsSTAT.pbs`: compute alignment statistics.

- `00_Subsampling_bam.pbs`: split a BAM into three reproducible subsamples.


For BAM subsampling, providing `TOTAL_READS` produces an exact, as-even-as possible split. Omitting it uses fast independent random assignment, so the three output files may have slightly different sizes.


2. EM-seq processing


The EM-seq PBS job is an array job. It selects the sorted `*_R1.fastq.gz` file corresponding to `PBS_ARRAY_INDEX` and derives the matching R2 filename. The reference genome is expected at:


```text

$DATAWORK/Epigenetic/Methylome/in/Vaestu_circlatorS15_12-016.fasta

```


Submit it after counting the input R1 files:


```bash

SAMPLE_COUNT=$(find "$DATAWORK/Epigenetic/Methylome/in/EMseq" \

  -name '*_R1.fastq.gz' | wc -l)

qsub -J 1-${SAMPLE_COUNT} \

  -v DATAWORK="$DATAWORK",SCRATCH="$SCRATCH" \

  01_Sequencing-DATA-processing/00_Scripts-PBS/02_EMseq.pbs

```


The wrapper runs trimming, Bismark genome preparation and mapping, BAM filtering/deduplication, methylation extraction, and coverage filtering.


3. m5C motif finding


`02_m5C_methylation_motif_finder/search_motif_V2.py` combines a reference genome FASTA, a context FASTA, and one or more Bismark coverage files. Samples are provided as `NAME:FILE` pairs:


```bash

python 02_m5C_methylation_motif_finder/search_motif_V2.py \

  path/to/reference.fasta \

  path/to/context.fasta \

  --samples \

    S15-1:path/to/S15-1.sorted.bismark.cov.gz \

    S15-2:path/to/S15-2.sorted.bismark.cov.gz \

    S15-3:path/to/S15-3.sorted.bismark.cov.gz \

  --output results_m5C.tsv \

  --spectre \

  --summary

```


The output is a tab-separated motif table. `--spectre` adds per-base methylation and coverage information; `--summary` writes an additional motif-level summary table.


Required methylome-table processing order


Run these steps in the order below. Use explicit input and output paths so that each stage can be reproduced and audited.


Step 1: Deduplicate methylation sites


`01_deduplication.py` removes duplicate or conflicting motif calls and writes Excel and TSV outputs, together with debug and discarded-row tables.


```bash

python 03_Methylome-table_processing/01_deduplication.py \

  -i results/01_annotation/annotated_methylome.tsv \

  -o results/02_deduplication

```


The input may be TSV, Excel, or Parquet. The main outputs include:


```text

annotated_methylome.deduplicated.xlsx

annotated_methylome.deduplicated.tsv

annotated_methylome.dedup_debug.xlsx

annotated_methylome.discarded.xlsx

```


Step 1bis: Merge EM-seq measurements


Run this step when EM-seq data are available. It transfers EM-seq signal columns to the deduplicated table for the supported CGCCG (m5C) and GGWCC (m4C) mappings.


```bash

python 03_Methylome-table_processing/01bis_merge_methylation_emseq.py \

  --deduplicated results/02_deduplication/annotated_methylome.deduplicated.xlsx \

  --emseq path/to/emseq_table.xlsx \

  --output results/03_merged/methylome.merged.xlsx

```


The EM-seq input must contain signal columns beginning with `methyl_rate.`, `avg_cov.`, or `methylated.` and the coordinate/motif columns needed for the join.


Step 2: Add methylation status


Run this step on the merged table, or directly on the deduplicated table when no EM-seq data are being used:


```bash

python 03_Methylome-table_processing/02_adding_methylation_status.py \

  -i results/03_merged/methylome.merged.xlsx \

  -o results/04_status \

  --classification-process old \

  --coverage-min 30 \

  --plot-ipd-distribution

```


The script produces status tables, PacBio metric tables, motif/replicate and motif/condition summaries, and optional IPD distribution plots.


Step 3: Annotate genomic context


`03_annotate_genomic_context.py` adds genomic context, defined promoter region information, gene identifiers, RGP information when supplied, and derived ratio/IPD columns. It exports `annotated_methylome.tsv` and JBrowse-compatible files.


```bash

python 03_Methylome-table_processing/03_annotate_genomic_context.py \

  -i path/to/methylation.tsv \

  -o results/01_annotation \

  --gff path/to/genome.gff3 \

  --promoter-size 200 \

  --jbrowse-prefix annotated_methylation_sites

```


Optional RGP annotation:


```bash

  --rgp-file path/to/rgp_coordinates.tsv

```


Use `--with-features` only when the input table already contains the required feature/context information and genome mapping should be skipped.


Supplementary coverage plots


`04_Supplementary_analysis/Coverage_plot_1.3.py` accepts one or more BAM files. Conditions are inferred from the filename prefix before the first underscore. For multiple BAMs, existing `.coverage.pkl` files can be reused or recalculated interactively when necessary.


```bash

python 04_Supplementary_analysis/Coverage_plot_1.3.py \

  path/to/control_sample.bam \

  path/to/treatment_sample.bam

```


The script calculates coverage in 1000 bp windows by default and writes the

static and interactive plots to `0_Coverage/`. BAM files should be indexed.


Reproducibility notes


- Record the reference genome, annotation GFF3, input file names, motif

  cutoff, coverage threshold, and software versions for every run.

- Keep intermediate tables from every table-processing step; do not overwrite

  the previous stage.

- Use absolute paths in PBS submissions and confirm that `DATAWORK`,

  `SCRATCH`, and `TOOLS` point to the intended storage locations.

- Inspect each script's built-in help with `python SCRIPT.py --help` before

  changing defaults.

- Several historical scripts contain cluster-specific absolute paths. Update

  those paths before running them on another system.

For support, contact Elyna Bouchereau at [elyna.bouchereau@outlook.fr](mailto:elyna.bouchereau@outlook.fr), or corresponding authors.

Bacterial Methylome Mapping

This archive is a complement to the scientific study Bouchereau, E. et al. “Environmental salinity drives DNA methylation

plasticity in the oyster pathogen Vibrio aestuarianus” (2027).


This archive contains the custom scripts necessary for processing PacBio kinetic data and EM-seq data, identifying methylation motifs (EM-seq), and producing an complete annotated methylome table. The exemples below use the directory layout used on HPC environment. Paths, module names and resource requests need to be adapted to user HPC environment and needs. - PacBio SMRT sequencing: used to detect m6A and m4C methylation from IPD

```text
        |

        |

Final tables and optional plots
```
